#6565. Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a big part of understanding the present-day Earth.

Earth is one big system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a new trick with them: photosynthesis.

Cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

But this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

New research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations."

The oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

The researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research shows that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on new geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide new constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

The researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

They found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

The second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

The researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

This graphic illustrates the results from new research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that shows how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

On shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it shows that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life."

This figure shows the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

It all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work shows that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

The pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

Understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the new treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

You can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This ethereal stainless steel set from Leif boasts pewter star-shaped handles with sea glass.

Even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice company’s new holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

When it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. There’s always a use for little glasses like this (and they’re pretty enough to display, too).

It’s pretty fun to use a posh plaid napkin when you’re digging into some quiche or sipping on mulled wine.

It’s always fun to kick off an evening of cocktails with a caviar bump, which is what makes this Imperia Caviar bundle such a gift for the avid party host. The 30-gram tin of royal ossetra comes with a mother-of-pearl spoon and a caviar tin opener in a velvet bag, and the bundle’s compact size means you can simply slide it into your purse or jacket on the way to the function (unlike a heavy bottle of wine or olive oil, which would likely need their owns bags).

It really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer. Nothing wrong with a traditional wood toothpick, of course, but it really does add a lot of pizzazz to a martini to bite the olives off a pearl-emblazoned skewer.

Swooning will abound once people get a look at these beautiful walnut chopsticks featuring inlaid geometric designs. Another great example of “practical, but nicer to look at than what you might get for yourself.” Plus, you can grab a set of five on sale right now for under $20.

When it comes to cocktail cherries, one brand truly reigns supreme: Luxardo, which has been making candied cherries soaked in marasca syrup for 120 years. A classic for a reason!

Jonathan Adler is another designer to keep tabs on when it comes to playful but elevated home decor. This set of Matisse-esque coasters also has a slight lip to keep condensation from spilling, and would be prime for serving up lychee martinis the next time you gather with friends. Snag them while they’re 40% off for Black Friday.

Halen Môn is a salt nerd’s dream. The organic, hand-harvested sea salt hails from the tides of the Isle of Anglesey in Wales (Halen is Welsh for salt; Môn is Welsh for Anglesey), and has earned numerous awards for its subtle crunch and crisp mineral flavor. Any host would be thrilled to receive a bag of the stuff, but this gift set combines the salt with a charming ceramic cellar and spoon.

Matches are always a solid host gift, and a small but useful present that’s made all the better with cool packaging. The lifestyle brand State the Label, for example, has housed its matches in a folk art-inspired cottage (the striker paper is on the bottom of the house).

Those who like to entertain likely appreciate a good placemat. This set of two block-printed placemats from West Elm puts a romantic spin on the dining-table staple with painterly tones and bright hues. Who wouldn’t love to receive these dreamy accents?

Is your host a lover of ice-cold martinis? Perfect gift incoming: Quincy’s fabulous olives, which have superb flavor and are ratioed with drink-perfect brine to make exactly 14 dirty martinis per jar.

Scents are tricky. Unless you really know your host, refrain from gifting them scented candles, and opt for a beeswax pillar candle instead; they can light it sans candelabra (unless you’re sure that they own one and prefer tapers) by simply placing it on a small plate. Above all, beeswax candles make a wonderful dining companion, because they don’t emit the same stuffy, paraffin wax-based smoke as non-beeswax candles.

Sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

We all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.

#6563. Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

Earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

Understanding why this is important requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

What was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study showed that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

Solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

With that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

Despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

Combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the new paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Stanford - Scientists discover sand dunes can reveal wind speeds on Earth and beyond

M. Colin Marvin et al - Windblown dunes are born in sand at the brink of transport [Author's note - PNAS page not fully indexed at time of writing]

#6561. This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

Binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs). It means that a body of gas surrounds both stars, but the gas doesn't move with either one separately. These envelopes are transitory; the CE creates drag that slowly draws the planets together, sometimes ending in an explosion. But it's difficult to predict when that will happen, and when astronomers should observe a particular binary star to learn more about it.

It all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. No two stars in a binary system are the same. One evolves and puffs up, overflowing its Roche lobe. Mass begins to pile up on its companion. That process becomes unstable, and the two stars become engulfed in a common envelope of gas.

The common envelope exerts a powerful drag on both stars, and they're drawn closer together. After that, the CE is ejected and the two stars are left behind in a compact binary. The pair of tightly-bound stars can remain as a compact binary, or they can merge and cause an explosion, called a luminous red nova(LRN). Whether they merge and explode, or whether they remain as a compact binary, depends on how soon the CE is ejected. If the CE isn't dissipated soon enough, the continued drag forces the stars closer together until they merge and erupt.

This simple graphic shows how common envelopes evolve. At first, on star fills its Roche lobe. Then, the companion is engulfed and both stars orbit one another inside the common envelope. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. Image Credit: By Philip D. Hall - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/55287112

This is a coarse overview of the process. Astronomers know it can happen, and they'd like to learn more about it. But they need to observe them, and that's tough to do. Not only are they difficult to predict, but they're also relatively rare.

Observations with the JWST and other telescopes have found one CE situation where a main sequence star a little less massive than the Sun spiralled into its CE partner, a puffy supergiant star, and erupted as a LRN. This happened in our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda. The observations and details are in new research in Nature titled "An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion." The first author is Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York.

"The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars," the authors write. "This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag."

That much is known by astrophysical theory. But nobody's observed the end of the inspiral and the eruption yet. "Here, we present observations of ATâ2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy," the researchers write.

Astronomers have lots of observations of ATâ2025abao with multiple telescopes because it's been experiencing brightness changes for several years and has attracted their attention. They've become familiar with ATâ2025abao and now simply refer to it as 'Bao'.

âStellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,â said first author Karambelkar. âHowever, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the starsâ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescopeâs data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.â

Stars in these situations orbit each other for thousands of years with little change, and that was true of ATâ2025abao. But once they contacted each other, things changed. Other stars in CEs take thousands of orbits before they merge. But this one was different from other CE binaries. The pair merged after only 7 orbits (about 7 years.)

Observations go back as far as 2018, and between then and early 2025, the star gradually brightened in optical light. After that, it gradually faded in optical light, but its infrared light continued to brighten. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. It brightened by 100 times in the r-band over a period 25 days, and its temperature jumped to about 8000 Kelvin. Then, for about 80 days it plateaued and cooled down to about 3000 Kelvin. The JWST observed it during this period, only 47 days after its peak.

âWe thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,â said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. âOne day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!â

âWhen a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect â a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Baoâs data,â said co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. âAs the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary starâs outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.â

This was when the CEE began. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward. This is when the JWST saw the destructive merger.

This is the finding chart for AT 2025abao. It was captured by the Asiago 67/92cm Schmidt telescope on 7 November 2025, when the light was at is maximum. M 31's (Andromeda) spiral disk is just visible on the left of the image. The zoomed-in panel shows the transient. Image Credit: Reguitti et al. A&A, 709, A25 (2026)

Since the transient has been in the watchful eyes of astronomers for so long, they have detailed spectroscopy from it. The SPHEREx near-infrared space observatory played an important role, catching the star in its survey. "In July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase," the researchers state. That let them determine the masses of the stars, but only with some help from simulations.

As in a lot of astronomy research, simulations played an important role here. In this research, the authors worked with different models of CEE until the outcome of one matched the JWST's detailed observations of the star and its surrounding dust, shed by the primary star over hundreds of years.

That work revealed that the primary was seven times more massive than the Sun, with a radius 350 times larger. It was also 18,000 times brighter than our star. âIt was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,â said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

The modelling also revealed the smaller star's true nature. It had only about 0.7 solar masses, one-tenth as massive as the other star. Its radius was much smaller and it was also much dimmer.

The astronomers called the pair Big Bao and Little Bao, and when Little Bao was engulfed, there was a massive explosion. Only more observations will reveal what the resulting star, now simply called Bao, looks like.

These artist's illustrations help explain what happened with ATâ2025abao and its common envelope evolution. The first panel shows the quiescent phase, when the stars are surrounded by a common envelope. The brightness was consistent during this phase. The second panel shows the stars brightening in the precursor stage. The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. In the third panel, there's a sudden bright eruption, as the companion spiralled and the common envelope is ejected. The JWST observed this. Then, in the final panel, months after the eruption, gas from the starâs ejected envelope freely expanded at the poles, but not at the equator, where previous ejecta from the more massive star was concentrated. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia)

"The 2025 eruption of ATâ2025abao displays the defining hallmarks of Luminous Red Novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion," the authors write. But it's different from all other known LRN. It's progenitor is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope.

"In contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence," the researchers explain. But classical CEE theory says that the primary star should be an AGB star.

"Thus, ATâ2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination," the authors explain.

Watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy. Astronomers have had to perform a sort of forensic astrophysical study of transients like this in other cases, trying to reconstruct what happened thousands or even millions of years ago. Even with powerful telescopes and computer simulations, and with detailed theoretical frameworks to guide their work, that's tough to do.

But this work opens a new window into CEE and how efficient it can be. And it's just in time to help with a potential flood of upcoming transient detections. Only a few dozen luminous red novae have been detected, but the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will detect hundreds of them, possibly thousands. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will also detect some LRN and CEE, but probably far fewer.

This work lays the foundation for understanding some of what those surveys will find. In a few years time, astronomers should have a much clearer understanding of common envelope evolution and luminous red novae.

"This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys," the authors write.

#6560. Experimental Drug Wipes Out Aggressive Pancreatic Cancer in 75% of Mice and Triggers Lasting Immunity

An experimental drug helped mice resist cancers their immune systems had never encountered, raising the possibility that treating one tumor could someday help protect against others.

Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most difficult cancers to treat, partly because tumors can wall themselves off from the immune system. Many breast, colon, and lung cancers use the same defense, surrounding themselves with dense, scar-like tissue that keeps cancer-fighting immune cells out. This barrier is one reason immunotherapy, which helps the immune system attack cancer, works for only a minority of patients with solid tumors.

Researchers have now developed an experimental drug that breaks through this barrier in mice. The treatment eliminated aggressive pancreatic tumors in some animals, prevented breast cancer from spreading, and produced lasting immune protection against future cancers.

The study, published November 9, 2026, in Cancer Cell, was led by Seong-Jin Kim, PhD, and scientists at MedPacto, Inc., in Seoul, Korea.

Tumors build their defenses partly by releasing large amounts of a chemical messenger called TGF-β. This substance encourages nearby cells to produce fibrous tissue while weakening the immune cells that could attack the cancer. Blocking it has proven difficult because TGF-β also performs important functions in healthy tissue. Previous drugs have struggled to suppress enough of it inside tumors without causing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

To get around this problem, the team developed a drug called FEBP-sTβRII that carries a molecular tag directing it toward tumors. The tag attaches to a particular form of fibronectin, a protein abundant in many cancers but rarely found in healthy adult tissue. Researchers detected this target in mouse models of breast, colon, lung, liver, prostate, pancreatic, and brain cancers, as well as melanoma, and in many human tumor types.

The targeted drug accumulated inside tumors and remained there for days. Without the tag, the same blocker had little effect on tumors and altered the activity of 693 genes in the blood, compared with just 25 for the targeted treatment.

“This study shows that where you block TGF-β matters as much as whether you block it,” said senior author Kim, who is also affiliated with the GILO Institute.

With the protective barrier weakened, cancer-killing T cells could enter the tumors. They released a chemical signal called interferon-gamma, prompting nearby support cells and immune cells to display recognizable pieces of the cancer. This helped the immune system identify its target and sustain the attack. Researchers observed this response in pancreatic tumors and melanoma.

Unlike existing immunotherapies that primarily remove restrictions on T cells, the experimental drug also changes the environment surrounding the cancer, making it easier for immune cells to reach and recognize tumors.

The researchers reported several promising results across different mouse experiments:

“TGF-β helps build the defenses of many solid tumors, so this approach has the potential to reach well beyond a single cancer,” said Dr. Letterio. “By delivering the blocker directly to the tumor, we don’t just open the door to T cells. We appear to be teaching the immune system lessons it remembers long after the tumor is gone, and in some cases those lessons protect against other cancers.”

Study co-author John J. Letterio, MD, PhD, directs the Angie Fowler Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Institute at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies & Children’s Hospital and the Developmental Therapeutics Program at Case Comprehensive Cancer Center, Case Western Reserve University.

The immune response observed in mice resembled patterns previously seen in patients who responded to immunotherapy for melanoma, gastric cancer, and pancreatic cancer. Measuring the drug’s fibronectin target in tumors might eventually help identify patients most likely to benefit.

A human version of the drug has entered safety testing, with clinical trials planned for 2027 to evaluate its safety and effectiveness in patients whose solid tumors have not responded to standard treatments.

Reference: “A stroma-sensing TGF-β blockade reprograms CAF-myeloid niches to induce durable tumor immunity” by Dong Woo Kang, Jin Beom Bae, Seonho Yoo, Hyejin Kim, Pyunggang Kim, Jaewoo Mo, Jinhwan Kim, Jin Su Kim, Kwiyeom Yoon, Ye Seon Kim, Jeong Su Lee, June Myoung Kim, Min Gi Kang, Min Jung Lee, Changwon Lim, Isaac Y. Kim, Chang Pyo Hong, Junil Kim, John J. Letterio and Seong-Jin Kim, 09 November 2026, Cancer Cell. DOI: 10.1016/j.ccell.2026.10.007

Disclosure: Dr. Kim is a founder of MedPacto and co-founder of Celloram. Dr. Letterio is a co-founder of Celloram and a member of MedPacto’s clinical advisory board. MedPacto holds pending patents on the drug.

Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6558. Sound Waves From Sunspots Launch Fiery Plasma Jets Across the Sun

It feels like every week for the past few months weâve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sunâs surface and its corona. This week is no exception, with a new paper in The Astrophysical Journal detailing the formation and tracking of around two hundred jet-like bursts of plasma from the surface known as âdynamic fibrils.â They serve as another piece of the puzzle of why the Sunâs outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.

The key to understanding this discrepancy, as weâve said before, is energy transfer. How does the pathway work for energy to come from the Sunâs interior to its upper atmosphere? At this point, the accepted answer seems to be through massive magnetic fields pushing plasma outwards and heating it intensely, but the nuances of the exact mechanism remain hazy.

Dynamic fibrils are one such potential mechanism. They are rhythmic jets erupting from the outer haloâknown as the penumbraâsurrounding a sunspot. But up until now we have had difficulty tracking where exactly they go, largely because the Sun is so bright it's hard to isolate individual tendrils from the overall burning mass of plasma.

Fraser attempts to answer why the Sun's corona is hotter than its surface.

To do so, Guotang Wu and Xiaoli Yan of the Yunnan Observatories at the Chinese Academy of Sciences combined data sources. They used the New Vacuum Solar Telescope, located in southwestern China, to monitor a sunspot in an active region of the Sun known as NOAA 13182. Crucially, they did so for just over an hour on January 10th, 2023, and took snapshots of the chromosphere â the middle layer between the Sunâs surface and its outer atmosphere â every 45 seconds. They then combined these ground observations with data from Chinaâs CHASE solar satellite and NASAâs Solar Dynamics Observatory, providing a multi-layered and multi-spectral view of this active sunspot.

Over that hour of observations, they catalogued 176 individual dynamic fibrils â jets of plasma that rise off the surface and into the Sunâs atmosphere. On average, they do so at a speed of 16 km/s, faster than the speed of sound in the surrounding plasma medium of the chromosphere. But eventually they slow down, falling back to the surface after an average lifespan of about 4.5 minutes. Even during that time, they manage to stretch on average 1,130 kilometers â roughly the distance from New York to Chicago.

So where do those jets come from in the first place? Sunspots are already famous for creating features known as ârunning penumbral wavesâ of compressed gas that move across the halo surrounding the sunspotâs core. According to math described in the paper, the rhythmic pulsing of the fibrils almost matches the five-minute cadence of the running penumbral waves in the sunspot. This, in turn, points to another underlying phenomena â magnetoacoustic waves.

Fraser talks about the highest resolution image ever taken of the Sun.

Under the surface of the Sun, hot convection cells of plasma constantly vibrate features known as âmagnetic flux tubesâ, creating low-frequency sound waves that leak upwards into the chromosphere. As the gas they are traversing gets thinner and thinner, they grow steeper and stronger until they âbreakâ in a similar manner to waves on a beach. However, these breaking waves are not like those of water â each breaking wave is accompanied by a miniature sonic boom known as a magnetoacoustic shock. These push the plasma residing in the chromosphere where they break, pushing chromospheric plasma upward to form dynamic fibrils.

Buried in the data there was a clear pattern of how much the orientation of these magnetic fields matters for the creation of fibrils. When the magnetic field lines point straight up, the plasma jets experience stronger deceleration and pulse at shorter intervals. Whereas when the fields lean more horizontally across the Sunâs surface, the fibrils decelerate more gently and pulse over longer periods. This confirmed a long-standing theory about how magnetic tilt affects solar sound waves.

To tie all this back to the original theme â extreme coronal heating â observations from SDO revealed corresponding signatures in gas heated to hundreds of thousands or even millions of degrees. So, the plasma pushed up by those shockwaves doesnât just appear to fizzle out - it directly transfers energy into the corona itself, which aligns with what many of the recent papers on this topic have been proving in various ways.

But weâre still not 100% sure of some of the nuances of how this complex magnetic dance actually works. That might have to wait for even bigger ground-based telescopes such as the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, which can resolve the magnetic threads inside these massive jets. But until then, we have an even clearer picture of how an acoustic hum plays a role in stoking the inferno of the Sunâs outer atmosphere.

#6557. Trump names Stephen Miller his chief of staff ahead of Dem takeover

Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, talks with reporters at the White House on April 28. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of the hard-line immigration and deportation program voters rejected this week, will become White House chief of staff.

Susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president's last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration's domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump said in a social media post.

Trump dubbed Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and said Wiles, who also oversaw his 2024 presidential campaign, “has done an outstanding job.”

Wiles, who Trump recently announced had won a battle with breast cancer, said in a X post that “serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding she was “proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

“I wanted to make a change,” he said in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Trump in recent days had become open to working with Democrats after the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3, even after railing against what he called the party’s “bad” policy during an October-long campaign rally blitz.

“Look, I mean, I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “But I have the power of the veto. So if we don't like what they're doing… They've already called and they want to talk about things. And that's fine.”

Trump summoned Thursday's press pool into the Oval Office for an executive order signing. On his desk was a red baseball cap with "VETO" across the front in large white lettering.

Miller has worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to several GOP lawmakers, including former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who became attorney general in Trump's first administration.

But making the hard-line Miller his White House chief of staff even before congressional Democrats get organized likely will draw the ire of the incoming majority.

Virginia Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr. was among the first Democratic lawmakers to slam Trump’s decision.

“Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller doubles down on the politics of hatred, lawlessness, and failure that the American people soundly rejected three days ago,” Beyer said in a statement. "Miller embodies the worst elements of the Trump presidency. His promotion shows that Trump has learned nothing from his electoral debacle and has no intention of even trying to work constructively with the next Congress.”

Many congressional Democrats — leaders, returning incumbents and members-elect — want to investigate Trump, his inner circle and family members while also pursuing a legislative agenda aimed at paring the cost of living.

To that end, as chief of staff, Democrat-run committees calling Miller to testify is highly unlikely since he could continue to claim executive privilege. That allows senior White House aides to withhold many internal West Wing communications, documents, and presidential-related conversations and actions, from lawmakers.

In public comments and television interviews, Miller has accused Democrats of being aligned with figures and candidates who “hate” Americans, and once said the party is “unworthy of power.”

“So the Democrats have become a party of freaks, weirdos, losers and crazies,” Miller said during a July appearance on Fox News. “But you can’t laugh it off because it’s deadly serious. When you give these people power, everything you know and love in this world falls apart. You have chaos, corruption, decay, violence, poverty.”

#6556. Why Sleeping 9 Hours After 50 May Be a Warning Sign for Your Career

More sleep does not necessarily mean more years at work, as a large Finnish study links both restless nights and unusually long sleep to shorter working lives.

As retirement ages rise and people are expected to work later into life, researchers are looking more closely at what helps people remain in the workforce as they grow older. A large Finnish study suggests that sleep may be part of the picture. Adults who frequently struggled with sleep after age 50 tended to spend fewer years working, while those who regularly slept nine hours or more a night also had shorter expected working lives.

People with severe sleep disturbances could expect to spend around eight fewer months in the workforce than those who rarely experienced sleep problems. Among people who slept at least nine hours a night, the gap ranged from roughly nine months to more than two years, depending on the study group.

The findings, published online in Occupational & Environmental Medicine, come as more than half of the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) have raised statutory retirement ages in response to aging populations. Previous research has explored why people leave their jobs early, including disability, illness, and retirement decisions. However, researchers had not examined whether sleep duration and quality were associated with how long people remain employed.

To investigate, the team focused on working life expectancy, which measures the average number of years someone can expect to remain employed at a particular age. Rather than measuring how long people live, the researchers examined their expected years in the workforce between ages 50 and 68.

The analysis drew on two Finnish studies involving more than 76,000 adults. The Finnish Public Sector (FPS) study included 70,339 public sector employees between 2000 and 2016, approximately 80% of whom were women. The Health and Social Support (HeSSup) study provided a random sample of 6,071 working-age Finnish adults between 1998 and 2013, with women accounting for 54% of participants. Researchers assessed sleep using the first survey each participant completed after turning 50, then examined employment information from the Earnings and Accrual Register, maintained by the Finnish Centre for Pensions.

The surveys asked participants how long they usually slept and how often they experienced difficulties falling asleep, staying asleep, waking too early, or feeling unrested after sleeping. These disturbances were assessed over the preceding four weeks. People who experienced them no more than once a week were considered to have no sleep disturbances, while those reporting problems two to four nights a week were placed in the moderate category. Severe disturbances meant experiencing these problems five or six nights a week to nearly every night. Sleep duration was classified separately as short, meaning less than seven hours, mid-range at seven to eight and a half hours, or long at nine hours or more.

The results revealed a consistent relationship between disrupted sleep and fewer expected years of employment. Participants without sleep disturbances had an average working life expectancy of 13 years and five months after age 50. That fell to approximately 13 years among those with moderate disturbances and 12 years and 10 months among those with severe problems. Compared with people reporting no disturbances, these groups could expect to work nearly five and eight fewer months, respectively. The association appeared among both men and women and across three broad occupational categories: professional, intermediate, and routine jobs.

Employment differences became more apparent when researchers examined sleep alongside occupation and sex. Professional women who reported no sleep disturbances had the longest expected working lives in this comparison, at nearly 14 years after age 50. Men in routine jobs who experienced severe sleep disturbances had the shortest, at approximately 12 and a half years.

Sleep duration revealed a somewhat different pattern. In the Finnish Public Sector study, participants sleeping fewer than seven hours a night and those sleeping between seven and eight and a half hours had the same average working life expectancy of 13 years and two months. Those who regularly slept nine hours or more, however, had an expected working life of just 12 years and five months. Compared with the mid-range sleep group, that represented approximately nine fewer months of employment.

The association was even stronger in the HeSSup study, where sleeping nine hours or more was linked to just over 30 fewer months of expected employment compared with sleeping seven to eight and a half hours. Researchers found no clear evidence that people sleeping fewer than seven hours had shorter working lives than those in the mid-range category, regardless of sex or job type.

Education and occupation also appeared to shape these patterns. When researchers compared the most advantaged participants, those with professional jobs or higher education and no sleep disturbances or short to mid-range sleep, with the least advantaged, those in routine jobs or with lower education and severe sleep problems or long sleep, the differences were considerable. The gap in expected working life was approximately one year and five months in the FPS group and five years in the HeSSup group.

In a more detailed analysis combining sleep duration with socioeconomic circumstances, 50-year-old men and women in professional jobs who reported short nightly sleep had the longest expected working lives in the FPS study, at around 13 years and seven months. In HeSSup, highly educated women had the longest working life expectancy, at approximately 11 and a half years. At the other extreme, men in routine jobs or with lower levels of education who regularly slept nine hours or more had an expected working life of only about six years and five months in both study groups.

Although the findings suggest a connection between sleep and working life, they do not establish that poor sleep or longer sleep directly causes people to leave employment earlier. The study was observational, and the researchers could not account for several potentially influential factors, including physical and mental health, underlying medical conditions, risky health behaviors, and working conditions such as shift work. These factors could affect both sleep patterns and the ability to remain employed.

Still, the findings suggest that helping people manage sleep problems in midlife may be worth considering as countries look for ways to support longer working careers, particularly among people facing socioeconomic disadvantages.

“Promoting sleep health and providing support for managing sleep disturbances at midlife may be especially important for those with a lower socioeconomic status when aiming to increase workforce participation with advancing age,” the researchers concluded.

“This could include cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia delivered by occupational health services or workplace interventions, such as educational or health promotion interventions for sleep.”

Reference: “Sleep disturbances and sleep duration as predictors of working life expectancy among adults aged 50 years and older in Finland” by Saana Myllyntausta, Katriina Heikkilä, Jaana Pentti, Holendro Singh Chungkham, Sakari Suominen, Mika Kivimaki, Jussi Vahtera, Paola Zaninotto, Jenni Ervasti and Sari Stenholm, 18 August 2026, Occupational and Environmental Medicine. DOI: 10.1136/oemed-2025-110766

#6555. What 8 Cool Food People Outsource for Thanksgiving

﻿Laila Gohar, Deb Perelman, and others share their top tips

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

Those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

“There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World

“I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the big stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen

“We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash

“I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most important one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

“Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World

“We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya

#6554. A Triple Star System 'That Shouldn't Exist,' Only 28 Light-Years from Earth

Sometimes astronomers search for one thing and find something completely different. There are many examples of that, from the Cosmic Microwave Background to Pulsars to Gamma-Ray Bursts. The same thing happened recently to researchers who were hunting for exoplanets. Instead of distant planets orbiting a distant star, they found an unusual triple star system in our stellar neighbourhood.

Their unexpected discovery is presented in a paper titled "WelopÅâai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. An international team of researchers made the discovery, and the lead author is Ãtienne Artigau. Artigau is from the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx) at the UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

âThe system should not exist.â - Professor Patrick Dufour, UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al.

âWe were actually looking for planets,â lead author Artigau said in a press release. âInstead, we found something much more surprising.â

IREx is the group behind Canada's contribution to the JWST, the FGS/NIRISS instrument. IREx's other instrumentation projects include the SPIRou and NIRPS high-precision infrared spectrographs, installed in Hawaiâi and Chile respectively, and the GPI imager on the Gemini-South telescope. This discovery began with the SPIRou (SpectroPolarimeter Infrared) instrument, which uses the radial velocity method to detect exoplanets tugging on their stars.

But in this case, instead of finding an exoplanet tugging on a star, they found another star tugging on a star.

"Serendipity has long played a key role in astronomy, offering insights into new phenomena," the researchers point out. "We report the serendipitous discovery of a white dwarf companion to the M4 V dwarf WelopÅâai Aa (IRAS 21500+5903) during a radial-velocity search for exoplanets with SPIRou," the authors write in their paper. "The system is located at 8.46 pc and forms a hierarchical triple with a more distant white dwarf, which has no known analogue within 30 pc."

Astronomers have watched the M dwarf, named IRAS 21500+5903 (also called TYC 3980-1081-1 A), and known about its unusual radial velocity (RV) signal since 2019. In this work, the researchers used SPIRou to gather almost five years of RV data on the red dwarf. That data showed that the RV signal had a large amplitude, which was inconsistent with an exoplanet signal. Exoplanets produce small wobbles as they tug on their stars.

"The mid-M dwarf showed a near-constant acceleration of approximately 5 m sâ1 dâ1 (â¼1800 m sâ1 yrâ1), a level inconsistent with a planetary companion: on a few-year orbit around a 0.42 Mâ star, even a Jupiter-mass planet would induce an acceleration of at most â¼40â130 m sâ1 yrâ1," the authors write.

That's math-speak for saying that the RV signal is up to 45 times stronger than a planet the mass of Jupiter could produce.

This figure shows the RV curve of WelopÅâai Aa from SPIRou observations spanning 4.8 yr, with the best-fit Keplerian model overplotted. The inset shows one week of observations, and shows how precise the measurements were. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321

Astronomers already knew that the M dwarf had a binary companion. It's a white dwarf, the massive dead core of a star that was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But that star is too far away to be responsible for the RV signal. Instead, another massive white dwarf was most likely close to the M dwarf.

âThe objectâs unusual combination of high mass and dim light left only one plausible explanation: it was the remains of a dead star,â said co-author Charles-Antoine Parent, a Mastersâ student at the University of Montreal. âThe most likely explanation was a white dwarf, although a neutron star or even a black hole couldnât be ruled out.â

To narrow it down, the researchers turned to the Gemini North Telescope and its âAlopeke instument. âAlopeke is a high-resolution imager that can eliminate distortion caused by Earth's atmosphere.

âAlopeke revealed the nature of the third star in the system, showing that it was a second white dwarf that forms an inner pair. "This inner pair lies at a projected separation of 123.9 au (Pâ>â1000 yr) from a previously known white dwarf," the authors write.

These panels show Alopeke observations in three different epochs, with yellow arrows showing the new white dwarf's position in December 2023 and 2024. It's more visible in some channels than others. The M dwarf is the central bright spot or region, it's shape distorted in the effort to highlight the white dwarf. Image Credit: Artigau et al. A&A Volume 715, November 2026 A321

Determining the mass of a solitary white dwarf is challenging. There are billions of them in the galaxy, but precise mass measurements of them are very rare. Only a handful of masses have been determined for nearby white dwarfs. Determining their masses in binary stars is easier, and because the new white dwarf interacts gravitationally with the red dwarf, the researchers could determine its mass dynamically, rather then depending on its brightness or its spectrum.

They found that the new white dwarf companion has about 0.62 solar masses. "The dynamically determined mass of the inner white dwarf is one of only a handful of such measurements for white dwarfs within 20 pc, and the most precise, at the sub-percent (0.7%) level," the researchers explain.

The system has been named WelopÅâai, a Hawaiian word that combines welo (an inherited or family trait) and pÅâai (an orbit or encircling path), together evoking a âpath of family traits.â The primary red dwarf is designated WelopÅâai Aa, its newly discovered close white dwarf partner is WelopÅâai Ab, and the outer white dwarf is WelopÅâai B.

This graphic shows observations of the WelopÅÊ»ai triple-star system, located only 28 light-years from Earth. The image on the left shows the two components of the system: WelopÅÊ»ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and WelopÅÊ»ai B, a second white dwarf much farther away. The image on the right is a close-up view of the inner pair, and it shows the faint white dwarf companion (Ab) that was detected with the Gemini North telescopeâs âAlopeke instrument. The overlaid curves illustrate the starsâ orbital paths. Image Credit: Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST (left); International Gemini Observatory/NSF

This system is very unusual, and rare. By determining its mass so accurately, the discovery will inform models of stellar evolution, something astrophysicists are always keen to improve.

âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises.â - Ãtienne Artigau, IREx, University of Montreal.

The new white dwarf was once a main sequence star like our Sun. But since it's so close to the red dwarf, the pair most likely interacted gravitationally at earlier stages of the white dwarf's evolution. It's possible that the two were inside a common envelope at one point, a situation where an envelope of gas surrounds both stars. That often forces the stars to spiral inward and merge. That should have destroyed WelopÅÊ»ai A, the red dwarf. But it appears to be intact, which is surprising. Somehow it survived that disruptive, turbulent scenario and follows a stable orbit.

âThe system should not exist,â says Prof. Patrick Dufour, white dwarf specialist at UniversitÃ© de MontrÃ©al and co-author of the study. âWe have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations.â

There are still some unexplained things about this system. The red dwarf is between 9 and 11 billion years old, yet is suprisingly metal-rich. Stars this old aren't expected to have such high metallicity. "Reproducing the metallicity would require the M dwarf to have captured roughly two-thirds of the metals, and almost none of the hydrogen or helium, ejected by the inner WDâs progenitor," the authors write, and there's no known mechanism that could do this.

"These puzzles, together with the still-open question of how the inner binary avoided a classical common-envelope in-spiral, identify WelopÅâai as a valuable benchmark for future work on binary-star pollution and tidal evolution," the authors write.

âDiscoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,â said Artigau. âEven when weâre searching for planets, our Universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us!â

#6553. New FDA-Approved Pill Lowers High Blood Pressure and May Slow Kidney Disease

A new drug targeting a hormone linked to hypertension has shown encouraging results in patients with chronic kidney disease.

A drug that showed early signs of protecting damaged kidneys has now received FDA approval for treating high blood pressure that remains uncontrolled despite medication. Called Baxfendy (baxdrostat), the treatment targets a hormone involved in both hypertension and kidney disease.

The approval follows Phase 3 clinical trials showing substantial blood pressure reductions. Earlier research also found that baxdrostat lowered a key marker of kidney damage by 55%, suggesting potential benefits beyond hypertension. Whether the medication can slow kidney disease progression remains under investigation.

The FDA approved AstraZeneca’s Baxfendy in May 2026 for adults whose hypertension remains inadequately controlled by existing treatments. It is the first approved aldosterone synthase inhibitor, a class of drugs that reduces production of the hormone aldosterone.

In the Phase 3 BaxHTN trial involving 796 patients, the 2 mg dose reduced systolic blood pressure by an average of 15.7 mm Hg after 12 weeks, compared with 5.8 mm Hg for placebo. The additional reduction of 9.8 mm Hg was statistically significant. A lower 1 mg dose also produced meaningful improvements.

Dr. Bryan Williams, Chair of Medicine at University College London and the trial’s primary investigator, said: “We have been waiting for an innovative medication like Baxfendy for hypertension for many years. Its novel way of lowering blood pressure has the potential to transform clinical practice by targeting a root cause of persistently uncontrolled hypertension. In addition, the nearly double-digit placebo-adjusted systolic blood pressure reduction achieved with Baxfendy is exciting and clinically meaningful for clinicians and patients. Epidemiological data indicate that a 10 mmHg decrease in systolic blood pressure is associated with a roughly 20% lower risk of serious cardiovascular events.”

Aldosterone regulates sodium and water balance in the body. Excessive levels cause the kidneys to retain fluid, increasing blood pressure and potentially contributing to kidney inflammation and scarring.

Baxdrostat inhibits the enzyme responsible for producing aldosterone rather than blocking the hormone’s receptors, as some existing medications do. This approach may benefit patients whose blood pressure remains high despite multiple treatments.

A separate Phase 3 trial, Bax24, involving 218 patients found that baxdrostat lowered average systolic blood pressure over 24 hours by 14.0 mm Hg more than placebo. The effect persisted throughout the day and night, according to findings published in The Lancet.

High blood pressure and chronic kidney disease can worsen each other. Elevated pressure damages the kidneys’ filtering structures, while declining kidney function makes hypertension harder to control.

“These findings are encouraging for people living with chronic kidney disease and high blood pressure, two conditions that often go hand-in-hand and create a dangerous cycle,” said lead study author Jamie P. Dwyer, M.D., a professor of medicine at University of Utah Health. “High blood pressure can worsen kidney function and declining kidney function can further elevate blood pressure, and these outcomes can be life-altering for patients.”

In the Phase 2 FigHTN trial, 192 patients with chronic kidney disease and uncontrolled hypertension were randomly assigned to receive baxdrostat or placebo alongside standard treatment. After 26 weeks, systolic blood pressure fell an average of 8.1 mm Hg more in the baxdrostat groups.

Researchers also measured urinary albumin, a protein associated with kidney damage when present in elevated amounts. Levels were 55% lower in patients receiving baxdrostat than in those taking placebo. The findings were published in the Journal of the American Society of Nephrology.

The earlier kidney disease trial found elevated blood potassium in 41% of baxdrostat recipients, compared with 5% of placebo recipients. Most cases were mild or moderate, but excessive potassium can cause dangerous heart rhythm disturbances. Serious adverse events occurred in 9% and 3% of participants, respectively.

Although subsequent Phase 3 hypertension studies reported no unexpected safety findings, potassium levels and kidney function require monitoring during treatment.

“The reduction in urine albumin gives us hope that baxdrostat may also help delay kidney damage. This potential is now being tested in two large Phase 3 trials to determine if baxdrostat delays the progression of kidney disease,” said Dwyer.

Larger studies are investigating whether baxdrostat can preserve kidney function over time, including trials combining it with dapagliflozin, an established kidney-protective medication. Its FDA approval currently covers hypertension, not the prevention of kidney disease progression.

“These new findings are reassuring that this new class of antihypertensive medications are likely to have both kidney- and cardio-protective benefits and to be safe and effective for broad patient populations,” said Jordana B. Cohen, M.D., M.S.C.E., immediate past chair of the American Heart Association’s Hypertension and Kidney Cardiovascular Science Committee. “Patients with chronic kidney disease were historically often excluded from drug studies. It is particularly reassuring to know that patients with chronic kidney disease, who have very high rates of hypertension and elevated renin-angiotensin aldosterone activity, were represented in their own study, tolerated the medication well, and had both blood pressure and albuminuric benefits. This medication class could be a game changer in the management of hypertension in this patient group.”

“Efficacy and Safety of Baxdrostat in Participants with CKD and Uncontrolled Hypertension: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial” by Jamie P. Dwyer, Noha Maklad, Ola Vedin, John Monyak, Robin Myte, Glenn M. Chertow, Hiddo J.L. Heerspink and Dustin J. Little, 6 September 2025, Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. DOI: 10.1681/ASN.0000000849
