#6514. Heart Stents May Not Prevent Heart Attacks or Early Death, Landmark Study Finds

A stent can restore blood flow to the heart, but in people with stable coronary disease, it may offer no added protection against heart attacks or early death.

For someone told they have a narrowed heart artery, opening it can seem like the obvious next step. Yet improving blood flow and preventing future health problems are separate goals, and a procedure that achieves one may not necessarily achieve the other.

Researchers led by Neel Butala, MD, of the University of Colorado Anschutz, examined that question through an extended follow-up of participants in the COURAGE trial. They found no statistically significant difference in the combined risk of death or heart attack between patients initially assigned to an artery-opening procedure plus medical therapy and those assigned to medical therapy alone.

Published in JAMA and presented at the 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Sessions, the findings offer an unusually long look at how these treatment strategies compare.

The original COURAGE trial enrolled people with stable coronary artery disease and compared optimal medical therapy alone with optimal medical therapy plus percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), commonly known as angioplasty.

During angioplasty, doctors inflate a small balloon inside a narrowed artery to improve blood flow. They often place a tiny metal tube called a stent to help keep the artery open.

For the new analysis, researchers tracked 959 participants through linked health records. The median follow-up was 15 years, with some patients followed for as long as 25 years. The estimated 25-year cumulative incidence of death or heart attack was 93.3% in the group initially assigned to PCI plus medical therapy and 91% in the medical therapy group. That difference was not statistically significant.

Earlier research had examined long-term survival after the trial. This analysis also included heart attacks, allowing researchers to assess whether an initial PCI strategy might prevent cardiovascular events that would not be captured by survival figures alone.

The central finding concerns what happens after an artery has been successfully opened. Restoring blood flow can relieve symptoms, but the study did not find evidence that starting with PCI lowered the combined long-term risk of heart attack or death.

“When we open a blocked artery, we know we’ve improved blood flow through that artery, and that relieves symptoms. But the bigger question is whether that translates into a reduction in clinical events such as heart attacks or death for patients over the long term. That’s what we wanted to understand with this study,” said Butala, an assistant professor of medicine-cardiology at the CU Anschutz School of Medicine.

“We found no significant difference in the risk of death or heart attack between the two treatment groups. That’s important information for doctors and patients as they consider the best approach to treating stable coronary artery disease.”

These results do not mean angioplasty and stents are unnecessary. They can relieve chest pain and other symptoms, while emergency procedures can be lifesaving during certain types of heart attacks. The study specifically examined an initial PCI strategy for stable coronary disease, so its findings should be understood within that setting.

Although the participants came from a randomized trial, this analysis was a post hoc observational follow-up, rather than a new randomized trial. It included veterans whose health records could be linked, a group with higher baseline health risks than the full COURAGE trial population.

The researchers also acknowledged limitations in identifying heart attacks through routinely collected health records. However, the findings were consistent with events independently verified during the original trial.

The research helps clarify what an initial procedure may accomplish. Symptom relief remains a meaningful benefit, but the long-term findings do not establish additional protection against heart attack or death compared with medical therapy alone. Butala said considering both immediate relief and future health outcomes can support more informed treatment decisions.

Reference: “Percutaneous Coronary Intervention and Long-Term Outcomes in Stable Coronary Artery Disease: Extended Follow-Up of the COURAGE Randomized Trial” by Neel M. Butala, Nandini Murali, Natalia Rahman, Shayna Cave, Siamack Ayandeh, Mary E. Plomondon, Jonathan W. Cunningham, William S. Weintraub, Robert W. Yeh, Stephen W. Waldo and William E. Boden, 7 November 2026, JAMA. DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.23488

#6510. Alzheimer’s Breakthrough: Researchers Find New Clues to Cognitive Decline in Healthy Adults

Researchers have identified a promising way to assess Alzheimer’s-related cognitive risks in otherwise healthy older adults.

A blood test could help estimate whether someone with no memory problems will develop cognitive impairment within the next five or 10 years. In a new Mayo Clinic study published in JAMA Neurology, researchers developed a method that combines an Alzheimer’s-related blood biomarker with age, sex, and genetic risk to produce personalized estimates.

For example, a 75-year-old woman without the APOE e4 genetic risk variant had an estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) of 5% when her biomarker level was relatively low. At a higher level, that estimate rose to 16%. Her predicted 10-year risk increased from 12% to 35%.

The method measures phosphorylated Tau 217 (p-tau217), a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Elevated levels in the blood are linked to Alzheimer’s-related changes in the brain, but a positive biomarker result alone cannot determine whether or when someone will develop cognitive symptoms.

“The goal is to provide a personalized estimate of the risk of developing cognitive impairment that is more meaningful than simply reporting whether a blood test is positive or negative for amyloid pathology,” says Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic laboratory medicine and pathology researcher and first author of the study.

The research builds on an earlier Mayo Clinic prediction model that used positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans to detect amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease. Measuring p-tau217 in blood offers a less invasive approach that could be used more widely.

Researchers analyzed data from 1,644 cognitively healthy participants in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All were between 60 and 90 years old and had undergone blood biomarker measurements, genetic testing, and repeated cognitive assessments.

Using the Mayo Clinic data, the team calculated the probability of developing MCI or dementia within five or 10 years. Higher p-tau217 levels and older age were associated with greater risk. At the same elevated biomarker level, the estimated five-year risk of MCI was 6% for a 65-year-old but 37% for an 85-year-old.

The researchers then examined the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative data, which independently supported the association between elevated p-tau217 and increased risk of cognitive decline.

The approach could eventually help doctors identify people who might benefit from preventive treatment before memory problems begin. However, its clinical usefulness will depend partly on whether therapies can successfully delay cognitive decline in people who have no symptoms.

“A person may want to know: What is my risk of developing cognitive impairment in the next five or 10 years, and how does this blood test change that risk?” says Ronald Petersen, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and director of the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging. “If preventive therapies prove effective, those numbers could become very important in treatment decisions.”

Clinical trials, including AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are investigating whether treatments targeting amyloid can delay cognitive decline before symptoms develop. Both trials have used blood biomarkers to help identify participants, highlighting their potential role in earlier Alzheimer’s research.

“Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context,” says Clifford Jack Jr., M.D., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and senior author of the study. “If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about the potential benefits and risks of treatment.”

The risk estimates were developed using the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and require further evaluation in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Although the findings support the potential of personalized risk prediction, Alzheimer’s biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without cognitive symptoms.

Reference: “Absolute Risk of Progression to Cognitive Impairment Based on Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217, Age, Sex, and APOE ε4” by Alicia Algeciras-Schimnich, Mingzhao Hu, Stephen D. Weigand, et al., 16 November 2026, JAMA Neurology. DOI: 10.1001/jamaneurol.2026.4292

Recently, researchers used AI to "decode" segments of birdsong. In the wake of this, Live Science asks its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The idea of talking to animals like Dr. Dolittle might sound far-fetched, but researchers are making progress toward understanding how other species communicate. In a recent Live Science interview, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie explained how she used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the calls of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata). For instance, Elie was able to determine which calls the birds used to communicate over short distances versus longer distances.

Birds aren't the only animals scientists are hoping to understand. Researchers with Project CETI are using AI to decipher the clicks and calls of sperm whales, while a separate team (with the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI) conducted what they described as the first "conversation" between humans and a humpback whale. The whale, named Twain, responded to recorded calls played by researchers over a 20 minute period, a "conversation" scientists believe could help us figure out how to communicate with extraterrestrial life someday.

Closer to home, cats have already figured out how to use meows to get their human's attention, whether they're demanding food, affection or simply that we open the door for them (again). Whether this means they understand the human language or not is still up for debate, but it raises an interesting question: If we could understand what animals were saying, which species would you most want to talk to? Vote in our poll and let us know what you'd ask in the comments below!

#6507. Scientists Develop New Nanomaterial That Could Help the Body Regrow Missing Bone

A biodegradable material developed by Australian researchers could eventually help children born with cleft lip and palate regrow missing jawbone without undergoing invasive bone graft surgery. In preclinical testing, the experimental nanomaterial produced approximately 80 percent more new bone than a control material after eight weeks.

Developed at the University of Sydney in collaboration with the University of Queensland, the material works by activating the body’s existing repair signals rather than supplying external growth factors. Researchers hope the approach could eventually allow children to receive treatment years earlier than is typically possible today.

Cleft lip and palate affects approximately one in 700 children and develops when parts of the upper lip or roof of the mouth fail to fuse completely during pregnancy. Correcting the resulting jawbone defects is among the most challenging aspects of treatment, with potential consequences for eating, breathing, speech, and social development.

“One of the biggest challenges for children born with cleft lip and palate is repairing the bone defect in the jaw,” said lead researcher Associate Professor Chun Xu, a Sydney Horizon Fellow in the University of Sydney’s Faculty of Medicine and Health.

“While some children with minor defects are treated as infants, many patients need to wait until they are around 10 to 12 years old before surgeons can take bone from another part of the body and graft it into the defect.

“That means many kids live with difficulties for years. It can affect their breathing, eating and speech. Most heartbreaking of all, it can have a huge impact on their confidence and social development.”

More than four million bone repair procedures are performed worldwide annually. Many current treatments rely on bone harvested from the patient or animal-derived materials that primarily provide structural support. The new approach instead aims to stimulate the formation of living bone using a biodegradable calcium-aluminosilicate nanomaterial.

The material activates a naturally occurring growth factor called latent Transforming Growth Factor β1 (TGF-β1). This protein normally exists in an inactive form until biological signals trigger its activity. Once activated, it helps recruit stem cells to the damaged area and encourages their development into bone-producing cells. As new tissue forms, the biodegradable material is gradually replaced by the patient’s own bone.

“The material activates dormant repair signals in the body, triggering a cascade of healing processes that attract bone-forming stem cells and stimulate new bone growth,” Xu explained.

“Our body already contains many of the signals needed for tissue repair,” Associate Professor Xu said.

“We’ve developed a material that can help activate those signals at the right place and time. Instead of supplying external growth factors, we’re encouraging the body to use its own healing potential.”

The study, published in ACS Nano, found that the material activated the body’s latent bone repair growth factor at approximately 10 times the level achieved using conventional methods. It also promoted blood clotting within about 30 seconds, which could help stabilize an injury during the earliest stages of healing.

According to the researchers, this is the first demonstration of a single nanomaterial platform capable of combining rapid blood clotting, activation of naturally occurring growth factors, recruitment of bone-forming stem cells, and enhanced bone regeneration. The findings come from a preclinical bone model, however, and further testing is necessary to determine whether the material can be used safely and effectively in humans.

Xu and his colleagues envision a future in which bone defects can be repaired earlier in childhood, potentially reducing the need to remove healthy bone from elsewhere in the body.

“Our long-term goal is to develop materials that help the body regenerate bone naturally and reduce the need for these invasive and painful procedures. We hope this could allow treatment much earlier than is possible today.”

The researchers are also investigating whether the nanomaterial could be incorporated into personalized 3D-printed scaffolds designed to fit an individual’s bone defect. Beyond cleft lip and palate, potential applications include repairing bone damaged by traumatic injuries, tooth loss, and other conditions involving difficult-to-heal defects.

“Every patient is different, and every bone defect is different,” Xu said.

“In the future, we hope to combine these materials with advanced 3D-printing technologies so treatments can be tailored to the specific needs of each patient.”

The technology remains at the preclinical stage, with additional research required before human trials can begin.

Reference: “Multifunctional Mesoporous Calcium-Aluminosilicate Nanoparticles Enable Heterogeneous Activation of Endogenous Transforming Growth Factor β1 and Rapid Hemostasis for Bone Repair” by Chun Xu, Qingxuan Chen, Hang Chen, Aoni Xu, Juan Wen, Yiwei Li, Huan Dai, Siyuan Liu, Dan Cheng, Yaping Song, Bing Sun, Jie Tang, Jie Fan, Chang Lei and Chengzhong Yu, 15 September 2026, ACS Nano. DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.6c05126

The authors acknowledge the funding support from Australian Research Council, National Health and Medical Research Council and the University of Sydney. A provisional patent application related to the findings reported in this manuscript has been filed by the University of Sydney and the University of Queensland. The application covers calcium-aluminosilicate mesoporous nanoparticles and their use for bone repair, as described in the paper (Provisional Patent Application No. 2026903515).

#6505. Does the Sun Have a Secret Companion? A Controversial Theory Could Explain Earth’s Mass Extinctions

A mysterious 26-million-year pattern in Earth’s extinction history has fueled a controversial theory involving an unseen stellar companion to the Sun.

Scientists have long believed that long-period comets with highly inclined orbits, some capable of causing mass extinctions on Earth, originate in the hypothetical Oort Cloud. This vast, roughly spherical reservoir of icy bodies is thought to contain trillions of objects and extend as far as 1.6 light-years from the Sun.

Richard Muller, a well-known professor emeritus of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, has proposed another explanation for why some of these comets enter the inner solar system. In addition to gravitational disturbances caused by passing stars, he suggests that a low-mass red dwarf star (dubbed Nemesis) could periodically redirect comets toward the Sun. Under this hypothesis, Nemesis and the Sun orbit a shared center of gravity.

According to Muller, Nemesis follows a slightly elongated orbit that periodically brings it into regions of the Oort Cloud, where its gravity could disrupt the paths of billions of comets.

Muller explained in a phone interview that these encounters could trigger comet showers lasting roughly a million years. The greatest number of comets would be redirected into the inner solar system when Nemesis passes through the cloud’s densest regions.

The proposed Nemesis star is not related to the hypothetical Planet X. It also differs from unrelated stars that occasionally pass near the solar system and gravitationally disturb the Oort Cloud, potentially sending numerous comets inward.

Unlike these unpredictable stellar encounters, the Nemesis hypothesis proposes a recurring cycle. Muller believes this mechanism could explain a pattern of impacts on Earth spanning approximately 250 million years.

Muller points to a 1982 study published in the journal Science by paleontologists David Raup and Jack Sepkoski. The researchers compiled an extensive record of marine extinctions that, according to Muller, revealed a striking pattern of extinction events occurring roughly every 26 million years.

The challenge was to come up with an explanation, says Muller. “Well, maybe there’s a companion star that comes close in to the Oort Cloud every 26 million years, and then triggers a comet hitting Earth,” he says.

It’s an idea that Muller still very much supports, although he isn’t sanguine about being able to directly observe Nemesis.

Despite what others seem to think, there is no clear evidence against this hypothesis, says Muller.

The Oort Cloud, a heretofore unseen, largely spherical cloud of comets and small icy bodies left over from the formation of our solar system some 4.5 billion years ago, very much remains a mystery.

There are three sources for the original material that formed the Oort Cloud, Astrophysicist Sean Raymond, Director of France’s Bordeaux Astrophysical Laboratory, told me via email.

Planetesimals that originated in our Sun’s planet-forming disk; planetesimals that originated around other stars in our Sun’s birth cluster, and interstellar objects that were captured during stellar encounters or by scattering by Jupiter, he says.

Many astronomers assume that if Nemesis is an ordinary red dwarf, somebody would have seen it, and the answer is no, because it’s moving with the Sun around the center of gravity. And as a result, Nemesis doesn’t show enough proper motion, or movement across our line of sight, to be detectable.

But it must be big enough to perturb the Oort cloud, which means it’s probably at least five percent the mass of the Sun, says Muller.

The consensus view is the K-T extinction event, which impacted the Yucatan Peninsula some 66 million years ago, was most likely caused by a large asteroid.

Yet the evidence that it’s an asteroid rather than a comet is very weak, so people say asteroid because that’s what Walter Alvarez, a professor of Earth and Planetary Science also at the University of California, Berkeley, said in his initial K-T Boundary paper, Muller notes. But when I asked Alvarez, I said, “You said asteroid. Could it be a comet?”

He responded, “Sure, we couldn’t tell the difference.”

The best near-term chance of characterizing this massive cloud, however, comes from the Rubin Observatory, which is just coming online. Astronomers hope that Rubin will be able to detect more long-period Oort Cloud comets.

The next comet shower that could cause serious damage to Earth should not be for another 12 to 15 million years from now, says Muller.

The bad news is that if it’s out there, Nemesis almost certainly would lie close to the plane of the ecliptic, which means that from our point of view, it would lie coplanar with most of the bodies of the outer solar system. And as a dim 8th or possibly 9th magnitude star, this would make it even more difficult to spot, certainly impossible to see with the naked eye.

So, Nemesis really is probably lost in a field of view that includes a huge number of other stars, says Muller.

References: “Dynamical Population of Comet Reservoirs” by Nathan A. Kaib and Kathryn Volk, May 30, 2022, arXiv. DOI: 2206.00010

“Measurement of the lunar impact record for the past 3.5 b.y. and implications for the Nemesis theory” by Richard A. Muller, 01 January 2002, Geological Society of America DOI: 10.1130/0-8137-2356-6.659

“Mass Extinctions in the Marine Fossil Record” by David M. Raup and J. John Sepkoski, Jr., 19 March 1982, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.215.4539.1501

Adapted from an article originally published in UniverseToday.

#6502. NASA Smashed Into an Asteroid. Now ESA’s Hera Spacecraft Is About to Reveal the Damage

The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera spacecraft has reached the two asteroids it was sent to investigate, marking a major milestone in a mission designed to strengthen Earth’s defenses against dangerous space rocks. Roughly the size of a small car, Hera is now traveling just 25 to 30 kilometers from the Didymos asteroid system, which consists of a larger asteroid and its smaller companion, Dimorphos.

The spacecraft has entered its initial observation period, known as the ‘early characterization phase’. During this stage, researchers are collecting essential information about both asteroids, with particular attention to Dimorphos, which NASA deliberately struck with a spacecraft in 2022 to test whether an asteroid’s path could be changed.

“Our aim right now is to gather the big-picture findings of relevance to supporting the mission’s planetary defense goals,” explains mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

“During this phase, our images will reveal for the first time what a small asteroid looks like globally, having experienced a hypervelocity impact in the context of the first asteroid deflection test, when NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted it to change its orbit in 2022.

“Previous predictions by our impact models suggested many different ways the asteroid body might react, but Hera will reveal which forecast was the correct one – if any!”

Navigating around two small asteroids presents challenges unlike those encountered by spacecraft exploring planets. The biggest difference is gravity, which is extraordinarily weak around these small bodies.

Didymos, the larger asteroid, measures approximately 780 meters across and has gravity roughly 40,000 times weaker than Earth’s. Its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, is about 151 meters wide, with gravity approximately 200,000 times weaker than Earth’s.

These conditions make a conventional circular orbit impractical. Instead, Hera moves around the shared center of gravity of the two asteroids at a remarkably slow speed of approximately 12 centimeters per second, comparable to a fast crawling insect.

Rather than continuously curving around its targets, Hera follows a series of nearly straight paths. During a repeating sequence of three days followed by four days, the spacecraft fires its thrusters while moving away from the asteroids, changing direction by 90 degrees. These carefully timed maneuvers produce a series of rectangular flight patterns that keep Hera approximately 25 to 30 kilometers from the asteroid pair.

The technique builds on lessons from ESA’s Rosetta comet mission. Its biggest advantage is safety. If a planned thruster firing fails, Hera will naturally drift farther into space instead of heading toward a potentially damaging collision. The slow flight speed also means that each course correction requires very little fuel.

Hera’s current observations are only the beginning. Next month, the mission is expected to enter its ‘detailed characterization phase’, bringing the spacecraft closer to the asteroids for more thorough measurements.

During this stage, Hera will begin following more complicated trajectories shaped like bowties. These paths, made up of hyperbolic arcs, will initially take the spacecraft to distances of approximately 20 kilometers from its targets.

The mission is directed from ESA’s ESOC mission control center in Darmstadt, Germany. Controllers communicate with Hera for approximately eight hours each day, despite the spacecraft being about 196.5 million kilometers away.

Those communications travel through four massive Deep Space Antennas, each measuring 35 meters in diameter, at facilities in Argentina, Spain, and Australia.

Supporting the controllers is ESA’s Flight Dynamics team. Specialists analyze information transmitted by Hera to pinpoint its location relative to the asteroids. They then calculate the commands needed to guide the spacecraft safely to its next position.

Hera’s primary scientific target is Dimorphos, which became the focus of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment on September 26, 2022.

That day, NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft collided with Dimorphos. The 580-kilogram spacecraft struck the asteroid at 6.1 kilometers per second, sending a vast cloud of debris spreading across approximately 10,000 kilometers of space.

The experiment achieved its main objective. The collision shortened Dimorphos’ orbital period around Didymos by approximately 33 minutes, demonstrating that a spacecraft could alter an asteroid’s motion through a direct impact.

However, the results also raised important questions. The change in Dimorphos’ orbit was significantly greater than scientists had predicted, suggesting that the asteroid responded to the collision in ways that existing models did not fully capture.

Researchers still do not know exactly how much physical damage the collision caused. Did DART create a large crater, or did the force of the impact substantially reshape Dimorphos? Scientists also need more precise measurements of the asteroid’s mass, composition, and internal structure to understand why the deflection was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential before the technique, known as ‘kinetic impact’, can become a dependable option for protecting Earth from a potentially hazardous asteroid.

Over the coming months, Hera will conduct a detailed ‘crash site investigation’ of Dimorphos, using its scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and the aftermath of the DART collision.

The spacecraft will also release two shoebox-sized ‘CubeSats’. These miniature spacecraft will approach the asteroids even more closely, gathering additional observations before the mission eventually progresses to landing operations.

Together, the measurements could reveal how Dimorphos absorbed and responded to the impact, helping scientists determine which predictions were accurate and why the asteroid’s orbit changed more than expected.

By turning NASA’s successful experiment into a better-understood planetary defense method, Hera could play an important role in preparing humanity to deflect an asteroid that might otherwise threaten Earth.

Nearly 50 years after launch, NASA's Voyager 1 probe will pass the one light-day mark on Nov. 18, a symbolic milestone for the agency's longest-running mission. Scientists reflect on the Voyager program's legacy and what comes next.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe, already the farthest human-made object in space, is about to set another record. On Nov. 18, the spacecraft will be so far from Earth that light, the universe's ultimate speed limit, takes a full 24 hours to reach it.

For researchers who worked on the Voyager program and continue to study its data, the symbolic milestone of being a full light-day from Earth celebrates a mission that continues half a century after it began. Since launching in September 1977, the twin Voyager probes have outlasted many of the engineers who built them, and their flybys of the outer solar system planets remain some of the best close-up observations scientists have of those distant worlds.

"Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are transcending generations," Pascal Lee, a planetary scientist at the SETI Institute who was part of the Voyager 2 team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) during its Neptune flyby in 1989, told Live Science. "Not only is their data relevant, but they themselves are still out there, moving into the unknown."

Here is what the Voyagers have revealed about the solar system and interstellar space, what happens when their power finally runs out, and whether anyone — or anything — might ever intercept the messages from Earth they carry.

A NASA simulation showing where Voyager 1 is relative to the sun and solar system planets.

Voyager 1, cruising through space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 km/h), is just shy of 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) from Earth. That's the distance light travels in 24 hours, also known as one light-day. The spacecraft will reach this milestone on Nov. 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. ET, after traveling through space for 49 years, two months and 11 days.

As long as that sounds, "it's still pathetically slow in the grand scheme of things," Lee told Live Science.

If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still.

Scientifically speaking, Voyager 1 hasn't even left its home neighborhood yet. In 2012, the probe traveled beyond the heliosphere, the bubble of plasma blown outward by the sun that shields the planets from incoming cosmic radiation. But it still remains within the sun's gravitational grasp, which extends past the Oort Cloud — a vast spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system. Voyager 1 will need about 300 more years just to reach the cloud's inner edge, and possibly 30,000 years to fly beyond it, according to NASA.

"If anything, it reminds us of the sheer vastness of space and time, and how this spacecraft is just a little mote of dust that's barely drifted out of the solar system still," Lee said.

On its current path, Voyager 1 will pass within 1.7 light-years of a dim star called Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years, at which point it will be closer to that star than to our own sun. Farther out, the nearest star system to our own, Proxima Centauri, sits about 4.24 light-years away — more than 1,500 times farther than Voyager 1 will be on Nov. 18.

Meanwhile Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, took a different route through the solar system after both probes launched in 1977, in order to swing past Uranus and Neptune after revisiting Jupiter and Saturn. Currently in interstellar space about 13 billion miles (21 million km) from Earth, Voyager 2 will reach its own light-day mark in November 2035, according to NASA.

An illustration of the Voyager probes passing beyond the heliopause, into interstellar space.

Crossing the one-light-day mark doesn't change how NASA communicates with the probe, though it does demand more patience.

NASA talks to the spacecraft using radio signals, which travel at the speed of light. At a distance of one light-day, a signal sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and a reply takes another 24 hours to make the return journey.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL, said in a recent statement.

As the spacecraft continues to cruise deeper into space, that wait will grow longer. Moreover, 50 years of traversing the solar system and the increasing distance from our sun takes a toll on the probe itself. Because sunlight in the outer reaches is far too faint for solar panels, Voyager 1 relies on nuclear batteries that convert heat from the natural decay of plutonium into electricity. That supply is gradually dwindling, prompting NASA to gradually shut down nonessential instruments to conserve what energy remains and extend the mission as much as possible.

Kelly Perry, a data systems engineer on the Voyager program at JPL, told Live Science via email that the mission team's priority remains the same: "keep the spacecraft going as long as possible."

A montage of planets imaged by the twin Voyager probes, showing Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Before the Voyagers launched, the outer solar system was largely a blur of telescopic speculation. The twin probes took advantage of a planetary alignment that comes around only once every 176 years, using the gravity of giant planets to slingshot themselves onward.

Together, they have discovered 23 moons across the outer solar system, revealed faint rings around Jupiter and captured the first detailed atmospheric profiles of Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. They also gave the first detailed, close-up views of Jupiter's moon Europa, transforming our perception of it from a blurry speck into a remarkably smooth, geologically young world — and now one of the prime candidates for finding extraterrestrial life.

We had no idea what they looked like. And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places.

Among the more striking finds, Voyager 1 spotted active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io in 1979, the first time they had been seen on any world other than Earth.

"We had no idea what they looked like," Lee said. "And all of a sudden they became places we could map, imagine ourselves exploring, landing on…they became places," he added.

"That's what Voyager was for me — a voyage of discovery," he said.

These discoveries laid the groundwork for decades of follow-up exploration, including NASA's Galileo mission to Jupiter and the Cassini mission to Saturn. Decades later, as the only spacecraft to return in situ data from outside the heliosphere, the probes also proved that interstellar space is a dynamic, complex frontier rather than an empty vacuum.

Each Voyager spacecraft launched with 10 science instruments. Today, only two remain active on Voyager 1 and three on Voyager 2, measuring the magnetic fields, plasma and cosmic rays of interstellar space.

NASA began switching off the others one by one decades ago to conserve power, including the camera on Voyager 1 just minutes after it snapped the famous "Pale Blue Dot" portrait of the solar system in 1990. Ongoing power-saving reconfigurations have since helped keep the aging spacecraft operational nearly 50 years into its lifetime.

Voyager's iconic "Pale Blue Dot" image shows Earth as a "mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam," in the words of Carl Sagan.

In one such recent effort, nicknamed the "Big Bang," engineers shut off certain high-power subsystems while switching on lower-power alternatives, which "bought us almost two more years during which we will not need to turn any instrument off," Perry said.

With onboard power steadily dwindling, however, "there's a recognition that it won't be forever," Deana Weibel, an anthropologist at the Grand Valley State University in Michigan who co-authored an upcoming book about the Golden Record aboard the Voyager probes, told Live Science.

Because Voyager is a science mission, its mission will be considered finished when "no science instruments are operational," Perry said. "The Science Team decided that the last remaining instrument will be the magnetometer," she added. "We will never intentionally power off this instrument."

After the science data eventually stops, both probes may still keep beaming back basic engineering updates, such as about their health and power status, until around 2036, according to NASA. Even after the spacecraft finally fall silent, they will keep coasting through interstellar space, and "analysis shows that they should remain intact," Perry said.

Scientists will still be able to calculate their positions based on their last known speed and trajectories, Weibel said. "We'll know intellectually where it is unless it gets intercepted."

An illustration of Voyager shown next to the Golden Record.

Theoretically, yes. But interstellar space is so unfathomably vast that the chances of aliens finding the probes are vanishingly small, Lee said.

That makes it unlikely that aliens will ever find the Voyager Golden Records — twin gold-plated discs meant to portray the diversity of life on Earth. They hold sounds such as wind and animal calls, greetings in 55 languages, images of our planet and a celestial map pinpointing its location — all intended for a hypothetical civilization capable of retrieving and playing them. (The probes also carry visual instructions for spinning the records).

In that sense, the Golden Records are as much an artistic exercise as a scientific one.

"The chances of us going after Voyager 1 and bringing it back for the Smithsonian — not that it's likely — are more believable than any chance of an alien civilization finding it, and then playing the record," Lee said.

Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort

If an extraterrestrial civilization did find the probe after we lost contact with it, "we would have no way of knowing," Weibel added. "It becomes something that's powered entirely by imagination at that point."

So why send a message at all? All three scientists interviewed for this story see the Golden Record as a cosmic time capsule, a symbolic gesture meant to unite humanity around a shared home planet. For all its imperfections, including the omission of some widely spoken languages and a few mislabeled tracks, the disc remains an enduring emblem of human presence on Earth, they said.

"Knowing that Voyager will continue its mission long past my lifetime actually gives me comfort," Perry told Live Science. "Although I won't be able to speak to the Voyager spacecraft any more, I love knowing that I'll always be able to look to the stars and know they're still on their way."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Space.com, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston. #6498. An Overlooked Property of Light Could Open the Door to a New Era of Optical Computing

Monitoring electricity in buried cables could one day become easier thanks to an overlooked magnetic effect in optical fibers, although researchers still need to overcome a major sensitivity challenge.

For decades, engineers have used optical fibers to measure magnetic fields around electrical cables, but these sensors generally need to wrap around the conductor to work. Now, researchers in South Africa have discovered that a magnetic field can also affect light when it points sideways across a fiber, challenging an assumption that has guided optical engineering for more than 50 years.

The finding, published in Optics Letters, could eventually lead to sensors that sit alongside electrical cables rather than surrounding them. It may also offer a new way to control light for optical computing.

MSc student Mohammed Raiyan Sharif and Professor Mitchell Cox at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University) in Johannesburg demonstrated the previously overlooked interaction, known as the transverse Faraday effect. Their research was conducted at the Wits Optical Communication (OC) Lab in the university’s School of Electrical and Information Engineering.

Optical fibers carry internet signals through thin strands of glass, but they can also detect magnetic fields. This sensing ability relies on the Faraday effect, first observed by Michael Faraday in glass in 1845. When a magnetic field points along the direction light travels, it slightly rotates the light’s polarization, or the direction in which its electric field oscillates. Measuring that rotation can reveal the strength of the magnetic field and the electrical current producing it.

A sideways magnetic field was not expected to produce the same effect. To investigate, Sharif and Cox placed strong magnets beside a stationary multimode optical fiber without touching it, then watched the light emerging from the other end.

Multimode fibers have relatively wide glass cores that allow light to travel along many different paths, repeatedly reflecting off the core’s mirror-like boundary. At the output, the overlapping waves create a pattern of bright and dark spots called speckle, similar to the shifting patterns inside a kaleidoscope.

As the researchers rearranged the magnets, a camera recorded changes in that pattern. The sideways magnetic field was somehow altering the light’s behavior inside the fiber.

“It wasn’t hard to 3D print a rig to test our intuition. Working out the theory for what we were seeing was the challenging part,” says Sharif. “The key was to return to the underlying equations and question assumptions that are usually taken for granted in fiber optics.”

The explanation involved a small part of the light wave that a widely used mathematical shortcut ignores. Known as the weak-guidance approximation, this approach assumes that light’s electric field oscillates almost entirely across the fiber, leaving out a tiny component that oscillates along its length.

The approximation works extremely well when the fiber’s core and surrounding glass have similar refractive indices, which describe how strongly a material slows light. However, Sharif and Cox tested step-index fibers, where the refractive index changes abruptly at the core’s boundary rather than gradually, as it does in graded-index fibers.

When that difference is large, the normally neglected longitudinal component becomes significant near the core’s edge. By including it in their equations, the researchers showed that a sideways magnetic field transfers some of the light’s transverse oscillation into the longitudinal component. This changes how light reflects inside the fiber and, ultimately, the speckle pattern it produces.

The team also distinguished the new interaction from the Cotton-Mouton effect, another response to sideways magnetic fields. The Cotton-Mouton effect increases with the square of the magnetic field’s strength, while the transverse Faraday effect increases in direct proportion to it.

Their measurements confirmed four predictions. The effect disappeared without a sufficiently strong step in refractive index, became stronger when light entered at steeper angles, occurred for only one polarization relative to the magnetic field, and varied with wavelength in the same way as the conventional Faraday effect.

With a magnetic field of 0.24 tesla, roughly the strength found close to a powerful neodymium magnet, light polarized across the field produced a speckle pattern only about 84% similar to the original.

“What is surprising is finding an overlooked, useful interaction in such a familiar technology,” says Cox. “It’s quite exciting that there is always something new to learn or discover, and often these things are right under our noses, hidden in the assumptions we have made for decades.”

One possible application is monitoring electrical currents with fibers laid alongside cables, including those buried in trenches. However, magnetic fields near most cables are much weaker than those used in the experiment, so the sensitivity of a practical sensor remains uncertain.

The researchers also envision replacing permanent magnets with electrical coils, allowing currents to control the patterns of light traveling through a fiber.

“Besides sensing, I think that being able to control different modes (patterns of light) inside the fiber electrically could unlock a new way to do optical computing,” says Cox. “We can model the way light gets distorted when it propagates through fibers, frosted glass windows, or even the atmosphere. If we change our perspective on those models, we can actually use light to do mathematical computations for us, for free.”

Reference: “Transverse Faraday effect in multimode fibers” by Mohammed R. Sharif and Mitchell A. Cox, 30 September 2026, Optics Letters. DOI: 10.1364/OL.611078

The research was supported by the South African Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and the National Research Foundation (NRF).

#6497. New Once-Daily Pill Slashes Bad Cholesterol by Nearly 65% in Clinical Trial

A pill taken before breakfast cut “bad” cholesterol by nearly two-thirds in a trial of people already taking statins.

High cholesterol can silently damage blood vessels for decades, increasing the risk of heart attacks and strokes without causing noticeable symptoms. Much of that danger comes from excess LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, which contributes to fatty plaque buildup inside artery walls. Although statins help millions of people control their cholesterol, some patients need additional treatment to bring their levels down.

A newly approved once-daily pill could provide another option. Lipfendra (enlicitide) reduced LDL cholesterol by nearly 65% in a clinical trial involving adults already taking statins. Approved by the FDA on July 16, 2026, it is the first oral medication in a powerful class of cholesterol treatments previously available only through injections.

Enlicitide targets PCSK9, a protein that influences how efficiently the liver removes LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream. Normally, PCSK9 promotes the destruction of LDL receptors on liver cells. When these receptors are lost, the liver becomes less effective at clearing circulating cholesterol.

By blocking PCSK9, enlicitide allows more LDL receptors to remain active, helping the liver remove additional cholesterol from the blood. Unlike earlier PCSK9 inhibitors that require injections, enlicitide uses a specialized macrocyclic peptide formulation with absorption-enhancing ingredients, allowing the medication to be taken orally.

A review published in Annals of Pharmacotherapy found that enlicitide reduced LDL cholesterol by 57.1% to 64.6% after 24 weeks across clinical trials. These reductions were comparable to those achieved with injectable PCSK9 inhibitors.

In a direct comparison involving patients already taking statins, LDL cholesterol fell by approximately 65% with enlicitide. By comparison, reductions were about 28% with ezetimibe and 6% with bempedoic acid, two other oral medications used to manage high cholesterol.

The review examined research identified through PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane through July 17, 2026. Participants included adults with elevated cholesterol and those with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, an inherited condition that causes unusually high LDL cholesterol levels from birth and increases the risk of premature cardiovascular disease.

In the largest trial, adverse effects occurred at similar rates among participants receiving enlicitide and those taking a placebo. However, a separate study involving people with inherited high cholesterol reported more diarrhea and dizziness among those receiving the medication. Longer-term monitoring will help establish its safety with continued use.

Enlicitide must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach. Patients may drink water, black coffee, or plain tea with the medication but must wait at least 30 minutes before consuming food or other beverages. A 30-day supply carries a list price of $315, although actual costs depend on insurance coverage.

While clinical trials have established that enlicitide substantially reduces LDL cholesterol, researchers have not yet determined whether it also prevents heart attacks and strokes. An ongoing cardiovascular outcomes trial is investigating whether its cholesterol-lowering effects translate into fewer serious cardiovascular events.

Reference: “Enlicitide: The First Oral PCSK9i for Lowering Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol” by Rachel C. Lucas, Mia E. Lussier, Azadeh Nasuhidehnavi and Taylor M. Clark, 14 October 2026, Annals of Pharmacotherapy. DOI: 10.1177/10600280261494015

#6495. How to make friends at freshman orientation

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for new member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”

Trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s new member orientation. Giddy, even.

The incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

“I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” said Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

Forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

“I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he said of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

“It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” said Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

Cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

“The congressman said that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s important that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

“This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke said. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

“I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” said Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

But just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” said Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

“I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he said.

After arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander said he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he said.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he said.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their new workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” said Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

“They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander said.

An unusual pair of seated figurines was discovered in a Stone Age grave in Romania in the 1950s.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Two Stone Age figurines ‪—‬ the Thinker and the Seated Woman ‪—‬ were discovered in a prehistoric cemetery in Romania.

In 1956, archaeologists unearthed two unique figurines from one grave while excavating a Stone Age cemetery in southeast Romania. The unusual figurines — known as the Thinkers of Cernavodă or the Thinker and the Seated Woman — were made by people from the Hamangia culture and may be linked to ancient astronomical beliefs.

The Thinkers of Cernavodă are in the collection of the National Museum of Romanian History and are a key part of the country's cultural heritage. They were crafted from fired clay and measure about 4.5 inches (11.5 centimeters) tall. The two figurines may represent a man (the Thinker) and a woman (the Seated Woman), according to the museum.

The Thinker sits on a low, four-legged stool. He bends forward slightly, rounding his back and neck, and his arms are bent. He rests his elbows on his knees and his head in his hands. This pose gives him a meditative quality, according to the museum, which is why he has been named after Auguste Rodin's famous 1904 bronze sculpture. The Seated Woman also has a long, bent neck and a small face. She has prominent hips, thighs and breasts. Her right leg is bent, and her hands rest on her knee.

The figurines are about 7,000 years old and were made by the Hamangia people, a Late Neolithic culture that stretched from the Danube River to the Black Sea. According to archaeologist Dumitru Berciu, who excavated the Cernavodă cemetery, the Hamangia culture lasted from about 5200 to 4500 B.C. The people focused primarily on sheep and goat herding, and they built defensive hilltop settlements. They also crafted spiral-decorated pottery and human-shaped figurines. But while Berciu found dozens of male and female figurines in the Cernavodă cemetery, he noted that both Thinkers were unusual for being depicted seated rather than standing.

The specific meaning of the Thinkers is unclear. Berciu suggested that the figurines were somewhat stylized, rather than realistic, because they served a magical or religious purpose. Since solar worship was common among later Bronze Age groups in Europe — as evidenced by artifacts like the Nebra sky disc from Germany and an ornate sun chariot from Denmark — Berciu interpreted the figurines as possibly connected to sun worship.

But the National Museum of Romanian History has suggested that the two figurines may have been made specifically as a pair, representing the complementary principles of masculine and feminine natures or a Neolithic family unit. Another interpretation is that the sculptures depict a pair of mourners who were buried with the deceased.

While the original meaning of the 7,000-year-old sculptures remains a mystery, people continue to be drawn to the contemplative pair, and the male Thinker figures prominently today in the logo of the National Museum of Romanian History.

#6492. A Major Review Reveals Three Antidepressants That May Outperform Prozac

A massive review of 30,000 people suggests three antidepressants may outperform Prozac, but the findings reveal how much remains unknown about long-term depression treatment.

A new review has found that some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found that people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta), and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

Treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants, so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real-world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The new review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six studies followed participants for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is important given the average time people take them is much longer.

Importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

Ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects, and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing, or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

#6489. Cerebral Palsy May Not Be What Scientists Thought It Was

New research is challenging how scientists understand cerebral palsy (CP). Of 515 genes previously linked to the condition, only 89 showed a statistically significant association in a new study, suggesting that many proposed genetic connections still lack sufficient evidence.

Published in the journal American Journal of Human Genetics, the research also proposes a different way to classify CP. Rather than treating it as a single disorder, the scientists suggest it may be better understood as a collection of symptoms arising from multiple underlying conditions.

Cerebral palsy is the most common motor disability in children, with up to 10,000 babies diagnosed in the United States annually. It has traditionally been associated with complications around birth, including premature delivery and temporary oxygen deprivation. However, genetic research over the past decade has increasingly pointed to inherited or newly occurring genetic variants as potential contributors. Unlike progressive neurological diseases, CP does not worsen over time, and rehabilitation and physical therapy can improve symptoms.

“There has been a lack of consensus on the definition of cerebral palsy and on the role of genetics in disease pathogenesis, leading to substantial variability in whether a child is diagnosed with CP,” says corresponding author Peter Robinson of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine and the Berlin Institute of Health at Charité.

“We have developed a paradigm that considers CP to be a phenotypic trait rather than a precise disease diagnosis. A better understanding of specific genetic variants has the potential to improve our understanding of the biology of the disease.”

To investigate the genetic basis of CP, the researchers evaluated evidence from 21 previously published studies involving 5,440 people diagnosed with the condition. These studies had identified potentially causal variants across hundreds of genes, but the new statistical analysis found convincing evidence of association for only a fraction of them.

“We decided to do this study because there has been no accepted statistical method to determine if a disease-associated gene is truly linked to CP,” says first author Adam Arterbery of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine. “We discovered it was extremely difficult to find statistical evidence of causality for many of the genetic variants previously linked to CP.”

The team also performed whole-genome sequencing on 460 children from 453 families receiving care at Shriners Children’s hospitals across the United States. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic genetic variants were identified in 70 families, spanning 60 genes. However, just 16 of those genes overlapped with the genes supported by statistically significant evidence in the analysis of earlier studies.

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not disprove connections between CP and the remaining genes. Instead, the available data are insufficient to establish those associations with statistical confidence. They propose viewing CP as a clinical characteristic that can emerge from different genetic disorders and environmental influences, rather than a single disease with a common biological origin.

“This framework could improve interpretation of genomic testing, help identify children who may warrant closer CP surveillance or specialist referral, and potentially identify genetic conditions requiring disease-specific management,” Robinson says. “But clinical utility and patient benefit will absolutely need validation before these findings can be applied to patient care.”

Future studies will focus on larger patient populations, prospective evaluations of clinical benefits and costs, and better access to genomic and medical data. “We hope our study will stimulate discussion about CP terminology, gene-disease associations, and variant interpretation,” Arterbery says. “The most productive response will be further validation and development of better genotype-phenotype evidence rather than treating the findings as a definitive list of CP genes.”

In recent animal tests, tiny robots released into the bloodstream showed promise for treating blood clots.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Microrobots controlled by magnets can sweep drugs towards hard-to-reach blood clots in the body, boosting the efficacy of these life-saving treatments, early tests in animals suggest.

In tests with pigs, the microbots helped to dissolve clots around 10 times faster than medication alone. The research team is now working on further safety testing to ready the technology for eventual human trials.

"The whole construct is inspired by nature," said lead researcher Simone Schürle, professor of medical microsystems at ETH Zürich. "There are these tiny bacteria that have little magnetic backbones which they use to navigate with the Earth's magnetic field, and we were really struck by the physics and the properties of them when exposed to rotating magnetic fields," Schürle told Live Science.

ETH Zürich announced the research in a statement on Nov. 9. It has not been described in a peer-reviewed study yet.

Left untreated, blood clots can cause life-threatening damage. These blockages can restrict the flow of blood to the body's key tissues, triggering serious cardiovascular events, such as heart attacks or strokes, which starve cells of oxygen.

Doctors can either remove clots manually with tools or deliver clot-dissolving drugs, called thrombolytics, close to the site of the blockage. However, getting these medications through the final few millimeters of their journey is often the hardest part.

"When a pipe becomes blocked in a branched pipe system, the fluid encounters greater resistance and instead flows through alternative routes where it can pass more easily," Schürle explained. "So when you then try to bring in drugs to dissolve the clot, they won't flow into this area because it's occluded [blocked off]."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This is where microbots can help. The bots are tiny particles whose movements can be controlled by external magnets, which send them rotating and tumbling through blood vessels. These bots can redirect the interrupted blood flow and thus carry essential drugs straight to their target, Schürle and her team say.

Each bullet-shaped microbot contains a magnetic backbone of iron oxide nanoparticles, which is surrounded by a protective sheath of hydrogel polymer. When exposed to a rotating magnetic field, the microbots essentially start to somersault through the blood vessel, creating little vortices that help carry the drugs along with them.

Crucially, the bots' rigid backbone ensures that they spin predictably, while the gel body prevents the particles from sticking together and forming a clump.

The researchers introduce the tiny robots into blood vessels where clots are present.

The robots' motion helps to direct blood-clot-dissolving drugs toward the clots in question.

The team first tested the microbots in a silicon model of a blood vessel that contained clots of pigs' blood. Aided by the rotating microparticles, a thrombolytic drug dissolved the blockages around 10 times faster than medication alone did. That's a potentially life-saving difference, the researchers said.

They then repeated the experiment in live pigs, placing clots in vessels in each of the animals' kidneys. "When we introduced our micro-robots with a conventional, state-of-the-art drug, we could reperfuse [restore blood flow to] a much larger area than if only the drug was there," Schürle said. "The next step is doing safety studies over a longer time and in larger animals."

Earlier safety studies in mice showed that both the iron oxide and the gel sheath polymer safely break down in the body within a few weeks. However, the team will now need to demonstrate that the device is safe in larger mammals before it can be trialed in human patients; their latest test in pigs did not look at how the device broke down or how the pigs fared after the clots were dissolved.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that the bots could be injected into the body alongside the thrombolytic medicine. Once inside, they'd be controlled by targeted electromagnets, making the technique easy to integrate into existing clinical procedures for treating clots.

The team's research is still undergoing peer review, but Schürle has applied for a patent for the microbots' production, which uses a droplet-based microfluidics technique to form each individual particle.

"It's a very cheap, high throughput method to produce the micro-robots," she said. "It's about improving the [clot-dissolving] procedure where it is lacking and helping the drugs travel the last millimeters to be really effective."

#6487. Redistricting battle could spill into 2028

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, here at the Capitol in January, wants to see his state's congressional map redrawn. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

House Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” said Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the new lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

New maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, said he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a new map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley said he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in New York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in New York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for new maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

It’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass new maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where new maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, said last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

In New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”

Democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their new majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to new maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he said.
