#6452. The 9 Best Ductless Air Conditioners for Efficient Home Cooling

Whether you want a budget-friendly option or a high-efficiency heat pump for year-round comfort, these are the best ductless air conditioners to consider right now.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Tired of using loud and unsightly window air conditioners or clunky and underpowered portable air conditioners? Even if you don’t have the means to install a fully ducted HVAC system in your home, you can still upgrade to a more powerful cooling system with a ductless air conditioner.

Ductless air conditioners, often called mini-splits, cool targeted areas of your home without relying on the ductwork. Instead, they connect a compact outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers, which are usually mounted on a wall or ceiling.

To help narrow down the best ductless air conditioners, I compared models across capacity, efficiency, installation requirements, noise level, smart features, and overall value. I also spoke with HVAC expert Kim Lincoln, who has 25 years of industry experience, for guidance on how mini-splits work, when they make sense, and what shoppers should know before buying.

To ensure that our list of ductless air conditioners caters to a wide range of needs, I looked at units from well-respected brands like Pioneer and Senville and selected models of various sizes at different prices. Many come with features like programmability, dehumidification settings, and, in a few instances, smartphone functionality.

As an added perk, most of these contraptions also double as heaters—which is useful during cooler months. I leaned on my experience with different types of cooling units, as well as product specs I reviewed during my research. The final list below represents the best in each category, including best budget and best for DIY installation.

For this update, I relied on the expertise of Lincoln, as well as my own experiences with several types of ductless air conditioners. I asked her a variety of questions about mini-splits, touching on topics like the differences between this type of air conditioner from other units, installation, and more. I also updated the products I recommend to reflect recent advances in smart home technology and energy efficiency.

This highly-rated AC unit from Senville comes in a number of sizes, ranging from 9,000 BTUs all the way up to 30,000 BTUs, and it comes in 120- and 230-volt models. It has 4-in-1 functionality, working as an air conditioner, heater, dehumidifier, and fan, and it operates at just 34 decibels, making it a tranquil option for a bedroom or nursery.

You can control all of its settings via the included remote. The air conditioner comes with an installation kit, including a communication cable and copper lines, but it’s important to note the brand requires professional installation for the unit’s five-year warranty to be valid.

This ductless air conditioner is perfect for small rooms and spaces, with a coverage that can handle areas between 200 and 500 square feet. Great for climate control storage and small bedrooms, the WYS009A-20 is an Energy Star-certified machine that’ll help you save money year-round. It cools as low as -13 degrees F and heats up to 122 F.

It has a permanent washable air filter and a remote control for easy operation—though you have to buy an additional remote to use Wi-Fi capabilities. It also operates at only 25 decibels, making it one of the quietest machines on this list, and it has four modes: cooling, heating, dehumidification, and ventilation. After installation, Pioneer provides free tech support and five-year coverage on replacement parts and the compressor.

This model from Della is a great value. It delivers 24,000 BTUs/hour, making it suitable for rooms up to 1,500 square feet. It’s also the sleekest model we found.

In addition to cooling, this unit has settings for heating, dehumidification, and ventilation, and that versatility extends to its selection of impressive features, including a 24-hour timer, sleep mode, energy-saving mode, and multiple fan speeds. You can easily adjust all of these using the included remote control and the Della+ app. The app allows users to control the settings, set timers, and control various Della units from one screen for whole-house control.

The Della Mini-Split comes with a full installation kit, including a line set, and it operates at 51 decibels. Some installers report the directions are confusing and have had to rely on online guides for extra help, but most reviewers are happy with this unit.

Suppose you want the ability to adjust your air conditioning from your smartphone. In that case, this model from Senville includes built-in Wi-Fi connectivity, allowing you to operate it remotely from an Android or iOS device.

It’s suitable for large spaces, thanks to its four-zone setup and 36,000-BTU output. Plus, it also has heating, dehumidification, and fan settings.

The unit has a turbo mode for even more versatility, and it automatically switches from cooling to heating based on the ambient temperature. The Senville Mini-Split comes with an installation kit that includes a 16-foot line set for your professional installer.

The large, rectangular indoor units that come with most ductless air conditioners can be a bit cumbersome on your wall, and if you prefer a more streamlined appearance, this unit uses a ceiling cassette instead.

The 9,000-BTU system can be used for heating and cooling in spaces up to 350 square feet, and it comes with a 16-foot line set and all necessary installation equipment. The system has a 24-hour timer, sleep mode, turbo function, and three indoor fan modes. It operates at 31.5 decibels, making it ideal for bedrooms.

If energy usage is your top priority, DELLA’s 12,000-BTU mini-split is one of the most efficient systems commonly available online. Its efficiency rating sits around 22–23 SEER2 (which is a newer efficiency standard that prioritizes real-world performance), and that means it uses significantly less electricity than many other entry-level mini-splits.

The inverter compressor automatically adjusts output instead of cycling on and off, which helps the unit maintain steady temperatures and reduces power consumption. (You’ll really notice this feature during periods of extreme weather that tend to spike utility bills.)

The unit is well-sized for bedrooms, offices, or small living areas, and it cools and heats spaces up to about 600 square feet. The built-in Wi-Fi control and quiet operation round out the package.

One drawback: While DELLA has great reviews, it’s a smaller company and may offer less customer support, based on some user feedback.

If you’re looking to cool a smaller space like a bedroom or home office, Costway Blast Series is a solid pick for a bedroom, office, or other small room where you want more permanent cooling than a window unit can provide. Its 9,000-BTU output is sized for spaces up to 450 square feet, so it’s a better fit for modest rooms than the larger 18,000- or 24,000-BTU systems in this category. It also offers quiet operation, a display-off function, a timer, and a remote control you can use from bed.

Like many of the units we looked at, this product is more versatile than a cooling-only AC, too. It has cooling, heating, dry, fan, and sleep modes, plus ECO, turbo, and iFEEL settings. The washable filter and self-cleaning function are also helpful for keeping routine maintenance manageable.

The tradeoff is that this model requires 208- to 230-volt power, so it may need electrical work before installation. Its 17 SEER2 efficiency rating is respectable, but not as high as some more expensive bedroom-friendly mini-splits. Still, for a smaller space, it offers a useful mix of performance, basic heat-pump functionality, and good value.

This high-efficiency mini-split system is specifically designed for DIY installation—and no special tools are required. It’s compatible with Google Assistant and Alexa, and it comes with features like an auto restart if there’s a power outage, leak detection, and sleep mode on the remote to adjust the temperature automatically during the night.

The unit heats and cools with 24,000 BTUs of power, which is more than enough, but considering the model's premium price, it's a little on the low side. Its SEER rating is 20.5, and operation is relatively quiet.

Overall, it’s a great package, albeit a pricey one.

Compared to window or portable air conditioners, ductless systems are more permanent, more powerful, and typically quieter. They also give you more control over specific rooms, so you can cool the spaces you actually use instead of the whole house at once. There are some drawbacks, though.

Ductless ACs run pricey (even setting aside the cost of installation). They’re also more visible than central air vents, and you need to size and place them carefully to cool a room evenly. DIY installs or wrong-sized units can cause issues in the long run.

Maintenance can also be difficult, as not all HVAC professionals are familiar with these products. However, for an older home with radiator heat (like mine is), it’s the best way to add efficient air conditioning without blocking most of our windows.

First, decide how many indoor units you need and where you’ll place them. Unlike window units, mini-split systems are permanent fixtures, so carefully consider where they’ll be most efficient within your home.

Generally, a single ductless air conditioner can handle cooling a targeted area or a single room. If you’re cooling down multiple rooms, consider a multi-zone system so that you get even temperatures throughout your home.

It’s also essential to select a unit that’s powerful enough for the room it’s in—too small and it may not cool your space. The cooling capacity of air conditioners is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTUs, per hour.

As a general rule of thumb, choose a unit that delivers 20 BTUs per square foot of living space. So, a 200-square-foot room needs at least a 4,000-BTU air conditioner. Those sensitive to noise should consider units with a quiet mode feature.

It’s also important to consider the electrical system in the area you plan to install the mini-split. Many larger mini-splits require 208- to 230-volt power, which works with both commercial 208V electrical service and the 240V circuits typically used for major appliances in homes, while smaller systems may run on standard 120V outlets without any needed upgrades.

Quieter units are more desirable for bedrooms, living rooms, and nurseries, where a peaceful environment is essential. Look for ductless air conditioners with noise levels between 19 and 30 decibels, since this range can be compared to the sound of leaves rustling or a soft whisper.

Units with levels between 30 to 40 decibels are still suitable for other areas of the home, since this range is comparable to background noise or casual conversation.

While shopping for your ductless air conditioner, you may see “SEER” with a number next to it. SEER stands for Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio, which measures how much energy your air conditioner uses during the annual cooling season. The higher the SEER rating, the less energy your unit uses to cool your home.

You may also see “SEER2,” a newer efficiency standard introduced in 2023 that uses updated testing conditions meant to better reflect real-world performance. SEER2 numbers are typically slightly lower than SEER ratings for the same unit, but they represent the same idea: higher numbers mean more efficient energy usage.

A product with an Energy Star certification has been rigorously tested by the United States Environmental Protection Agency for its energy efficiency. EPA-recognized laboratories test products to Energy Star specifications to ensure manufacturers produce energy-saving products.

Although testing guidelines change per product category, all items must prove they consume less energy than standard models without compromising performance.

Mini-splits are more permanent and expensive than window or portable air conditioners, so they make the most sense when you plan to cool the same space for several seasons. Most systems also require professional installation, and larger units may need electrical upgrades before you can install them.

They’re also not invisible. The indoor air handler usually stays mounted high on the wall year-round, which may bother homeowners who prefer the low-profile look of central air vents. Proper sizing and placement matter, too, since an oversized, undersized, or poorly positioned unit can lead to uneven cooling, wasted energy, or poor humidity control.

Ductless air conditioners cool your home without using the network of ducts that central HVAC systems rely on, says Lincoln. “The way I explain ductless cooling to homeowners is simple: the system conditions the room directly instead of trying to send cooled air through ductwork first,” she explains.

Instead, ductless air conditioners connect a small outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers using refrigerant lines. Because there’s no ductwork involved, these types of units are often more efficient and easier to install in older homes, additions, or finished spaces where running ducts would be difficult. They also allow for “zoned” cooling, meaning you can control the temperature in individual rooms instead of conditioning the entire house at once.

These systems are also more customizable than a whole-house system. “Where mini-splits really shine is zoning,” explains Lincoln. “One outdoor unit can support multiple indoor heads, so different parts of the house can be conditioned based on how those spaces are actually used.”

Yes. “A mini-split is just a ductless system made up of an outdoor condenser and one or more indoor air handlers,” says Lincoln. The terms ductless air conditioner and mini-split are generally used interchangeably, as we have in this guide.

Both describe systems that pair an outdoor condenser with one or more indoor air handlers connected by refrigerant lines instead of ductwork. The “split” part refers to the system being divided between indoor and outdoor components.

Some mini-splits provide cooling only, but many modern models are actually heat pumps, meaning they can both cool and heat your home using the same system. Adding air conditioning to an older home that previously utilized radiator or baseboard heat can be tricky—squeezing ductwork into closets and unused corners feels a bit like remodelling Jenga. These units solve that issue without much fuss.

Usually, yes. In most cases, it makes sense to hire a professional. Installing a mini-split usually involves mounting indoor and outdoor units, running refrigerant lines, and making electrical connections, which is why many manufacturers recommend professional installation.

“Installation is where good equipment gets made—or wasted,” advises Lincoln. “Mini-splits look deceptively simple once they’re on the wall, but installation is not casual work. Line sets, electrical, drainage, vacuuming the system down properly before startup…those are the steps that determine whether the unit runs the way it was engineered to run.”

Some systems are more DIY-friendly, but even those can be complicated if you’re not comfortable working with electrical systems or HVAC equipment. Professional installation also helps ensure the system runs efficiently and may be required to maintain the manufacturer’s warranty. If you are a very seasoned DIY pro who’s handy with a YouTube tutorial, you might be okay. Otherwise, we recommend budgeting for an installer.

Companies size mini-splits systems based on BTUs, which measure how much heating or cooling power the unit can deliver.

“When people ask how to calculate the right BTU for a room, the honest answer is that manufacturer charts are a starting point, not a finish line,” says Lincoln. “For a window unit, those charts can get you close. For a mini-split, a proper load calculation is the better answer.” This is another reason it’s great to work with an expert installer before ordering—they can guide your purchasing based on your needs.

Lincoln explains that it’s not a straightforward calculation, in most cases. “Room size is only the starting point. Sun exposure, ceiling height, insulation, window size, window direction, occupancy, and heat from electronics or appliances all change the cooling load,” she adds.

Smaller systems around 9,000 BTU often work for bedrooms or small offices, while 12,000–18,000-BTU systems handle larger living areas. As a rough rule, most homeowners look at units sized for the square footage of the space they want to heat or cool, but must consider all of these other factors, too.

#6451. What the Trump administration’s focus on AI and quantum means for science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Research on the technologies is thriving, but some scientists worry about what’s been displaced

On October 8, 2026, President Trump unveiled his administration’s new federal science priorities.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Many fields of science have struggled under the second Trump administration, with funding cuts and delays plaguing research in fields such as public health and climate science. But some topics have found firmer footing, including artificial intelligence and quantum science.

These technologies, along with supercomputing, “are going to be the three legs of the stool that is going to transform how science and engineering is done,” says Darío Gil, undersecretary for science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In November 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to launch the Genesis Mission, a $5 billion whole-of-government effort to advance science via artificial intelligence. The initiative began with the DOE but has since expanded to more than 15 federal agencies.

In June, the president issued an executive order that aims to accelerate the development of tools such as quantum computers, quantum sensors and quantum networks. And in July, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy issued a 123-page report describing its vision for a “golden age” of federal science, in which agencies align investments in research and development with administration priorities.

Federal agencies spent some $4.2 billion on AI R&D in 2025, according to an arm of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy that quantifies such investments.

Many scientists are enthusiastic about the opportunities for AI and quantum research. But some caution that a measured approach is needed. “My strongest opinion … is that I want to see all fields of science supported,” says Brad Marston, a physicist at Brown University and president of the American Physical Society. “Priorities have to be chosen, but getting a good balance is important, because you never know where some advance will come from.”

Through Genesis, the DOE plans to use its troves of data as well as experimental and computing facilities to produce a common set of AI tools and a shared ecosystem for science. “That’s conceptually a very powerful idea,” says astronomer Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. “And if it pans out as intended, it could drive great advances in science and technology.”

This year, DOE funded nearly 300 projects through Genesis — including one led by Mandelbaum. Her team’s effort aims to unify immense datasets from astronomical facilities around the world, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument and the Zwicky Transient Facility. That would enable AI models to be trained on the data, which could help uncover hidden astronomical insights.

H. Stockebrand/RubinObs/NOIRLab/AURA/SLAC/DOE/NSF

Other projects include efforts to accelerate nuclear reactor development, create simulations of the U.S. electric grid and study nuclear fusion. And federal agencies including the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health have launched their own Genesis efforts, centered around the mission’s National Science and Technology Challenges, which include topics in health, biology, energy, space, national security and more.

Many scientists were already wielding AI in their work. But Genesis “really did create an inflection point,” says John Sarrao, director of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, Calif. SLAC is now involved with 20 Genesis projects and leads two.

Compared with AI, quantum technologies are less mature. With quantum computing, “we’re still at mile one or two or three of a marathon,” says Celia Merzbacher, executive director of the Quantum Economic Development Consortium, a coalition of public and private institutions that works to bolster quantum tech in the United States. Nevertheless, researchers hope the two technologies can amplify one another. AI could help design and develop quantum computers, for example, while quantum computing shows promise for efficiently tackling certain machine learning problems.

Accordingly, several Genesis projects involve quantum error correction, quantum sensors and quantum materials. And the DOE’s Quantum Genesis initiative aims to develop scientifically useful, error-corrected quantum computers by 2028.

AI and quantum were not always hot topics. “Both of those areas … were kind of backwaters until recent advances,” Marston says. Before the development of deep neural networks, for example, AI was mostly a curiosity. “It points to the importance of having a balanced approach to science funding,” he says. What starts as an obscure scientific specialty may suddenly explode into wide relevance.

In the context of limited resources, prioritizing one area of research necessitates deprioritizing another. While some funding for the DOE’s portion of Genesis came from the One Big Beautiful Bill passed in 2025, much of the rest came from the DOE’s budget.

As excited as Mandelbaum is about Genesis, she is concerned about funding for non-AI related work. A cosmology grant her group received from the DOE didn’t align with Genesis mission priorities and was reduced this year, she says. “If the reality is that some of this [funding] is coming out of the baseline research budget in my field, then I think that it would be beneficial for the DOE to engage the scientific community about those trade-offs,” Mandelbaum says.

In response to these concerns, Gil says that the money going to Genesis from the DOE’s Office of Science — about $400 million so far — is small compared to the office’s total FY2026 budget of $8.4 billion.

Sarrao says that it’s important to build on the momentum of Genesis while still supporting the DOE’s core research. His impression is that things are trending in the right direction. “Are there really exciting opportunities? Yes, 100 percent,” Sarrao says. “Are there risks if you get the balance wrong? Equally well, 100 percent.”

#6450. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

California Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6449. Satellites watched a cluster of thunderstorms become Cyclone Xavier

Satellite images show how quickly Tropical Cyclone Xavier developed a distinct eye as it strengthened near the northern Cook Islands.

Today’s Image of the Day features Tropical Cyclone Xavier spinning over the South Pacific near the northern Cook Islands.

Bands of white clouds curve around the storm’s eye. In satellite images from a few hours earlier, the eye was still forming.

The MODIS instrument aboard NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this scene at 4:53 p.m. Cook Islands time on November 16, 2026.

By then, Xavier’s strongest sustained winds were estimated at about 120 miles per hour.

The clouds would tighten around a storm that was still gaining strength.

A few days earlier, the system that became Xavier was a loose cluster of thunderstorms.

In microwave satellite images from November 14, its structure was hard to make out.

By late November 16, distinct rainbands curved around a well-defined eye.

A separate sequence from the GOES-18 weather satellite shows the eye becoming easier to pick out over the course of hours.

The difference between those views comes down to what each instrument can see.

A daylight image like this one shows sunlight reflected by clouds and the ocean.

High clouds can hide the circulation beneath them, making it difficult to tell where a developing storm is centered.

Microwave observations can reveal parts of the rain structure beneath those clouds, giving forecasters another way to follow a storm as it organizes.

The eye is typically the calmest part of a mature tropical cyclone. Air sinks there, which helps keep clouds from forming.

Just outside it, warm, moist air rises in a ring of thunderstorms called the eyewall. That ring is usually where the storm’s strongest winds are found.

Farther from the center, the sweeping bands visible from space can bring bursts of heavy rain and wind, with quieter stretches in between.

Someone on an island can experience several rounds of rough weather as successive bands pass overhead, even when the eye stays out at sea.

From above, the bands look like parts of a single spiral. On the ground, they can feel like a series of separate storms.

The ocean beneath Xavier was about 84 degrees Fahrenheit, warm enough to supply plenty of heat and moisture. Winds also changed relatively little with height.

That meant there was little wind shear to tilt the storm and push its thunderstorms away from the center, allowing them to build around the same developing circulation.

Xavier also formed near the southwestern edge of a broad stretch of unusually warm water associated with El Niño.

During El Niño years, cyclones in the Southwest Pacific tend to form farther toward the central Pacific, shifting where island communities are most likely to encounter them.

Xavier developed on the eastern side of the international date line, near the northern Cook Islands.

The storm eventually reached Category 5 on the scale used in the South Pacific. As it moved west, it encountered drier air and stronger wind shear and began to weaken.

On Manihiki, one of the northern Cook Islands, the rain kept falling after the winds began to ease.

A resident told Pacific Media Network that some homes had lost sections of corrugated roofing and that electricity remained a concern.

The island was relying on solar power after losing its main diesel generator more than a year earlier, and the storm’s persistent cloud cover made it harder to keep batteries charged.

Emergency generators helped residents keep essential supplies cold. The island had also begun preparing well before Xavier appeared on satellite maps.

Each October, the island council begins removing hazardous coconut trees near homes and roads, a practice shaped by the damage Cyclone Martin inflicted on the northern Cook Islands in 1997.

Aqua passed over Xavier once that afternoon, catching a brief moment when the storm’s eye was in clear view.

On Manihiki, one of the most consequential features of the storm was the cloud cover that lingered after the worst winds had passed.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin, using MODIS data

Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China are revealing that at least two lineages of early humans were present in the region around 184,000 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Homo erectus was adaptable enough to live in rainforests in what is now southern China and may have lived alongside Denisovans there, two new studies hint.

The research is based on the incredibly rare findings of nine fossil teeth from ancient humans — eight from H. erectus and one from a mystery human in the genus Homo. The teeth reveal that H. erectus lived in China much more recently than previously thought and that this population likely devoured tropical food found there.

"I think it's exciting because it means that there are two hominin populations occupying these rainforest conditions there at the same time," study first author Frido Welker, a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, told Live Science.

H. erectus is generally seen as the first human species to venture out of Africa, after evolving about 2 million years ago. It spread through eastern Eurasia, reaching China and Indonesia between about 1.6 million and 1.8 million years ago. It is one of the longest-surviving hominin species, and the last known record of it is from 108,000 years ago in river flood plains in Java, Indonesia. However, there was no physical evidence of H. erectus being on the Asian mainland more recently than 400,000 years ago.

But in two caves in Guangxi province in southern China, researchers have found thousands of mammalian fossils, accumulated there by porcupines that scavenged for and collected bones. The Baxian and Naxian caves are about 9 miles (15 kilometers) apart, sitting in a karst landscape of limestone formations that are prone to dissolving to create caves that would have offered crucial shelter for H. erectus.

The entrance to Naxian Cave, as seen by a drone, is the tall and wide opening of a cave that goes back around 330 feet (100 meters) to a fossil chamber.

Researchers found the nine human teeth among more than 18,000 fossils, including from apes, elephants, rhinoceroses and other ancient hoofed animals, Welker and his colleagues reported in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature.

Radiometric dating of the fossils and surrounding sediments by methods including assessing the decay of uranium, pins them to about 324,000 to 184,000 years ago. Eight of the teeth have physical features reminiscent of H. erectus, but the ninth is more elusive. It looks distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals and modern humans, Welker said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Welker's team took samples from five teeth ‪—‬ four from the group that seemed to be H. erectus and one from the mysterious tooth ‪—‬ to see which ancient proteins were present, since DNA tends to degrade more easily than the proteins in an organism. (The study of these proteins is known as proteomics.)

The four similar ones had protein signatures that matched what had been seen before in H. erectus.

"The morphology is nicely confirmed by the proteomics," Welker told Live Science. Three of these teeth were from males, and the other was from a female, which the team was able to determine based on the presence or absence of amelogenin-Y, a protein coded for only by the Y chromosome.

Researchers investigating two caves in China have found nine human teeth, eight of which have been confidently identified as belonging to Homo erectus.

However, some parts of the protein signatures differed from what had been seen in other H. erectus remains in China, so the new specimens may be from a previously unknown H. erectus population that perhaps had a slightly different genetic makeup, Welker said.

The finding that H. erectus was present in mainland Asia until at least 184,000 years ago — rather than 400,000 years ago — fills a geographical and chronological gap, helping to explain how H. erectus was on Java 108,000 years ago.

"This brings the history of H. erectus in East Asia closer in age to the late Javanese examples, raising the possibility that these populations were connected through land bridges at times of lowered sea level," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who wasn't involved in the study, previously believed that specimens from the past 400,000 years or so flagged as H. erectus were actually Denisovans ‪—‬ ancient humans who lived in Asia, disappeared around 30,000 years ago and belonged to the Homo longi lineage. But he told Live Science that the new morphological and protein findings provide convincing evidence that H. erectus did survive until relatively recently in some places.

The fifth analyzed tooth, known as PA1796, remains mysterious. The protein analysis revealed it was from a male, but it didn't show a recognizable signature in the protein sequence data. Therefore, Welker's team suggested it could be from another hominin species that was present in the region at the same time.

Welker didn’t want to speculate about which species it might be, but said: "Sequence-wise it doesn't have this Homo erectus substitution and morphologically, it doesn't look like an erectus tooth."

The tooth could be from a previously unknown human species, but many experts suspect it is from a Denisovan.

"With some of the new material probably dating to less than 200,000 years old, this already brings it close in age to known or putative Homo longi/Denisovan samples in southern China and Laos, implying potentially long overlaps between these species," Stringer said. "Tooth PA1796 could represent a longi/Denisovan, though it is relatively small in size, and relevant comparative data for longi/Denisovans is sparse."

The entrance to China's Naxian Cave, which has a small opening and goes back around 164 feet (50 m) to a fossil chamber.

Recent research suggests there was interbreeding between the H. erectus and Denisovan lineages, and the new evidence increases the likelihood that this happened, at least occasionally, Stringer said.

Any firm conclusions of who the tooth is from will have to wait for further finds of similar teeth elsewhere, Welker said.

Hawks agreed that the tooth is most likely from a Denisovan, perhaps from a divergent branch for which we don't have protein data. But it could also be from a novel H. erectus population or someone from the same population as the other teeth who, for developmental or genetic reasons, wasn't typical. "I would have liked to see additional comparisons in the paper to more Denisovan teeth," Hawks said.

In another paper, also published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature, Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, and her colleagues examined trace elements in the same teeth, as well as in animal teeth from the caves, to see what they revealed about the hominins' diet and local habitat.

Their analysis indicated that this H. erectus population found plants and animals to eat in tropical, rainforest-like ecosystems. Previously, it was thought that only our own species, Homo sapiens, was able to adapt to this type of environment.

"Rather than being confined to open woodland and grassland environments, H. erectus was considerably more ecologically adaptable than many of us have assumed," Stringer said.

"Being adaptable and being flexible are not traits that we associate with ancient human species — these are traits that we associate with H. sapiens," Westaway told Live Science. "Suddenly we're seeing H. erectus being able to survive in environments that we didn't think they could possibly survive in."

And given the mysterious tooth, it is possible that two different early human populations were this adaptable, said Welker, who was a co-author of the study.

A view from Naxian Cave in China, where Homo erectus teeth were found.

Westaway and her colleagues also looked at levels of the element strontium in the teeth, which can shed light on where someone grew up based on the unique strontium levels in water and foods they consumed as children. The team matched these strontium levels to another karst landscape about 200 miles (320 km) away, in the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

"It looks like H. erectus moved across large areas, traversing this karst landscape in the rainforests" ‪—‬ a finding that adds to our understanding of these ancient humans, Westaway said.

It's absurd that people often think of H. erectus as an unsuccessful species, she added. "We think they were the first to leave Africa, the first to use fire. It blows my mind because they survived six times longer than H. sapiens has survived so far, so I don't see them as unsuccessful."

Hawks' big question, however, is linked to modern humans, who were in the Chinese region from at least 45,000 years ago.

"Denisovan DNA is present in the peoples of Island Southeast Asia, so, modern humans must have run into Denisovans at some point," he said. "If H. erectus was enduring in the same area at the same time, might H. sapiens also have encountered late H. erectus?"

#6447. A dead star sends out radio signals every eight minutes, then goes quiet for a day

A white dwarf beside a Sun-like star sends out radio pulses every 7.9 minutes, the first of its kind found with such a companion.

When a star like the Sun dies, it leaves behind a dense core called a white dwarf. Astronomers found one that sends out a burst of radio waves every 7.9 minutes during a roughly six-hour window.

It’s the first known radio-pulsing white dwarf with a Sun-like companion.

Radio-pulsing white dwarfs have been seen before, but every one with a known partner had a small, dim red dwarf beside it.

Small shifts in when the pulses arrive revealed the radio source moving with the white dwarf. That places the source on or near the star itself.

Sam McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist at the SKA Observatory, led the work.

The research was conducted at the Curtin University node of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research in Western Australia, with six colleagues in Australia, Spain, the United States, and Britain.

In an interview with Earth.com, co-author Natasha Hurley-Walker was asked what surprised her most when the team saw the white dwarf moving.

“We were extremely excited!” she said. “We knew immediately that this would be an independent test of our hypothesis that it was the orbital geometry that was causing the radio waves to appear and disappear every 32.5 hours.”

The source turned up in a survey of the Milky Way with the Murchison Widefield Array, a field of radio antennas in the Western Australian outback.

On December 4, 2024, it produced a run of bright pulses, each under four seconds long and spaced 7.9 minutes apart.

Over the next nine months, the array caught 214 of them. The MeerKAT telescope in South Africa added 33 and fixed the position precisely enough to match it to a star in the Gaia catalog.

Spectra from the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii showed that star to be a G-type star. Its surface is near 9,400°F (5,200°C), and it has about 94% of the Sun’s mass.

The system, cataloged as GPM J071507−114153, is roughly 11,000 light-years away, with a wide margin of error.

A pulse every 7.9 minutes is too fast for an ordinary star to spin without flying apart. So the pulsing object has to be something compact: a white dwarf or a neutron star.

Many follow-up observations caught nothing at the predicted times.

When the team sorted the hits and misses, a second rhythm appeared. The pulses are only on for about six hours, and that window comes around every 32.5 hours.

The team interprets the 32.5-hour cycle as the orbital period and the 7.9-minute spacing as the white dwarf’s spin period.

The researchers think the stars’ positions in their orbit determine when the pulses reach Earth.

The timing gave them more. If the radio source orbits with the white dwarf, its distance to Earth changes as it goes around. Its pulses should then arrive a few seconds early on one side of the orbit and late on the other. They did.

Hurley-Walker said that delay is what let the team say where in the orbit the waves are made. Without it, she said, they could have been coming from the pair’s common center of mass, which doesn’t move.

The companion’s spectrum shows it swinging at no more than about 110,000 miles per hour (50 kilometers per second). Combined with the delay, that caps the mass of the compact object.

The cap is too low for a neutron star, so the team settled on a white dwarf.

Astronomers call these objects long-period transients, radio sources that switch on and off over minutes to hours. The first one was found in 2021. The paper counts a dozen, four of them confirmed as a white dwarf paired with a red dwarf.

Theorists built their models for how the pulses arise on that pairing, with the red dwarf’s wind and magnetic field feeding the white dwarf.

A G-type companion in a 1.3-day orbit is a counterexample, and the authors wrote that the models will need to stretch to include it.

Hurley-Walker said the find also opens a different door. A Sun-like star outshines a white dwarf in visible light, so pairs like this one are hard for optical telescopes to pick out.

“Radio telescopes can now find these binaries that optical telescopes would have struggled to detect, which gives astronomers a new window on understanding binary systems,” she told Earth.com.

The MeerKAT pulses carried another clue. The orientation of the radio waves, known as their polarization, rotated the most when the white dwarf passed behind its companion.

That can happen when radio waves pass through magnetized gas. The pattern resembles what spacecraft have measured near the Sun’s corona.

“What we think is happening is that the radio waves from the white dwarf are passing through the magnetic field of its stellar companion,” Hurley-Walker said.

The authors left a second explanation open. A mass ejection from the companion could have crossed the line of sight by chance, since only 14 pulses had a usable twist measurement.

How the white dwarf makes the pulses is still unknown. The team has almost no handle on its magnetic field, and the distance to the system is uncertain by thousands of light-years.

The two arrays that found it are both forerunners of the Square Kilometre Array, now being built in Australia and South Africa, and McSweeney is helping commission the Australian half.

Hurley-Walker said she is designing surveys for it to find more of these systems and to test where they are, how fast they pulse, and how bright they get.

The detection software that found this one, she added, was written by Curtin doctoral student Csanád Horváth.

Until those surveys run, this eight-minute pulse beside a Sun-like star is a single system, and the modelers have to explain it.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Astronomy.

#6445. When should women start thinking about heart disease? Earlier than you might expect

New guidance explains how first periods, pregnancy complications, and menopause can offer clues to a woman’s heart disease risk.

Picture a heart attack and you probably picture a man in his fifties clutching his chest.

Yet heart disease kills more women in the U.S. than breast cancer and lung cancer combined, and much of what sets a woman’s risk happens decades before menopause.

New joint guidance from four medical societies tells doctors to start reading that risk at a girl’s first period.

The guidance comes as three papers from the American Heart Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

It’s built from existing evidence rather than a new trial, so it reorganizes what doctors already know instead of adding a new finding.

Sadiya Khan, a cardiologist at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, chaired the writing group. In an interview with Earth.com, she compared it to saving money.

“You would never wait until retirement to start saving. We should bring that same thinking to heart health,” Khan said.

Standard cardiovascular risk calculators already account for sex, but they don’t capture every risk factor tied to a woman’s reproductive history.

The new framework splits a woman’s life into four stages set by her hormones. They are the years around the first period, the decades of regular cycles, the transition into menopause, and the years after it.

Pregnancy counts as a separate event, running from 12 months before conception to 12 months after delivery.

Estrogen and progesterone act on blood vessels, heart muscle and the brain, not only on the reproductive organs.

Because those hormones rise and fall about once a month, with no equivalent in men, blood vessel function and sleep vary in the same rhythm.

The authors wrote that risk in each stage is shaped by the stages before it.

Asked by Earth.com which stage is most overlooked, Khan said the biggest gaps are what happened earlier, such as irregular or heavy periods, pregnancy complications and a diagnosis like endometriosis.

Those shape heart health in later stages, she said, and belong in the conversation at every visit.

“Heart health for women doesn’t start at menopause,” said Amanda Perak, a pediatric cardiologist at Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago who worked on all three papers. “Puberty is a big turning point.”

A first period before age 10 is linked to higher heart disease risk later in life, and the 2026 cholesterol guideline already lists it as a risk enhancer.

Some irregularity is normal in the first one to three years. A pattern that persists can signal the hormone disorder that used to be called polycystic ovary syndrome, which often comes with insulin resistance and unhealthy cholesterol.

The disorder, now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, affects an estimated 10% to 13% of women.

Heavy periods affect 20% to 30% of young women, and about half of those with heavy bleeding are low on iron. The authors wrote that menstrual patterns may be the earliest sign of heart risk a doctor can see.

Mental health turns in the same years. By about age 17, girls have at least twice the odds of a depression diagnosis as boys.

Teens with depression are more likely to develop obesity later, and the reverse holds too. Nearly one in five girls in organized sports consider quitting over menstrual concerns, the authors wrote.

“The goal isn’t to worry teens about the chance of a heart attack, which are decades away for nearly all of them,” Perak said.

“It’s that the teen years are when patterns get set, and it’s much easier to keep good heart health than to get it back.”

Estrogen levels in pregnancy rise to about 30 times their peak in a normal cycle, and the heart and metabolism both change to support the fetus.

The authors call it a stress test because it can expose risk that was already there.

Nearly nine in ten women ages 20 to 44 begin pregnancy with less-than-ideal heart health.

High blood pressure in pregnancy, gestational diabetes and preterm birth are each linked to higher heart disease risk later in life.

Mood and anxiety disorders affect up to 37% of women in the first three months after delivery.

The year after a birth is a vulnerable time for follow-up. Women move from obstetric care back to primary care, and that handoff is often missed.

The guidance notes that the obstetric threshold for hypertension, a systolic reading of at least 140 or a diastolic reading of at least 90, matches the cutoff for stage 2 hypertension in general adult care.

Perimenopause begins at a median age of about 47 in the U.S., and the authors describe it as a period of swings rather than a steady decline.

LDL, the so-called bad cholesterol, rises during the transition independent of aging. Hot flashes affect 50% to 80% of women in this stage, and about one in three report significant depression or anxiety symptoms.

Women then spend about 40% of their lives after menopause. Around 67 million American women are 50 or older, and an estimated 6,000 more reach menopause every day.

Menopause that arrives early carries extra heart risk of its own.

Hormone therapy can help manage menopause symptoms, but the authors advise against using it to prevent heart disease.

Years of unhealthy habits may begin to show in this stage as heart disease. Stacey Rosen, the association’s immediate past volunteer president, said it is never too late to do something about it.

“It’s always about opportunities,” Rosen said.

A woman may see a pediatrician, a primary care doctor, an obstetrician, a cardiologist and a psychologist over her life, and their notes rarely travel with her.

One of the three papers surveyed 70 leaders of women’s cardiovascular centers and heard back from 33.

Of those programs, 29 are in cities and one is rural, and the paper proposes a national network of centers that combine the specialties.

Khan told Earth.com the papers are a first step toward giving every clinician the same playbook.

The next change, she said, is connecting all the clinicians on a woman’s care team through the life stage framework.

Her advice for the next appointment was a single question. “Ask at every life stage: What is my heart risk, and what should I do about it now? It is never too early to talk about your heart health,” she said.

The framework rests on evidence that links these stages to risk, and the papers say plainly where the links are weakest.

It isn’t known whether treating severe hot flashes lowers heart disease risk, with or without hormones. Female-specific cutoffs for heart imaging tests aren’t yet in guidelines.

And none of the three papers reports a trial showing that sorting care by life stage, rather than by age, prevents more heart attacks and strokes.

Khan said she is especially interested in reaching younger women now that risk can be estimated up to 30 years ahead with the association’s PREVENT equations.

Whether clinics can be rebuilt around that forecast is the test the four societies have set themselves.

The research was published in the journal Circulation.

#6444. What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Kratom is a plant, but souped-up products derived from it can have strong and dangerous effects

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a new set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.

Kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up new versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.

Now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.

Kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, says Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.

In the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi says. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.

The leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most important is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.

Mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.

“It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” says Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”

Mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, says Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.

What nature made, chemists and users are happy to tweak.

As the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann says, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.

When people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.

While 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.

What is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving users in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.

It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman says.

Sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she says. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.

Patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she says. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. In 2025, U.S. poison centers documented 3,434 kratom-related exposure reports, reported both by people who called the center and medical professionals. “I see less fentanyl and more kratom at this point, or more 7-OH,” Sethi says.

In July of 2026, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily classified some kratom derivatives as Schedule I drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential and no medical use. Those derivatives include 7-OH and another related kratom derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl or MGPI, as well as MGM-15 and its powerful sibling MGM-16. The DEA re-upped the temporary scheduling of MGM-15 and 16 and MGPI in October. 7-OH was temporarily placed in Schedule I at any dose higher than that found in the kratom plant. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also issued statements warning consumers not to use the products. None of these measures affect the legality of the kratom leaf itself.

Regulations vary at the state level: Twenty-six states don’t regulate kratom at all, while six states and the District of Columbia list kratom’s ingredients as a Schedule I controlled substance, like the current federal scheduling. A further 18 states regulate sale and manufacture in some way.

“I think there’s a lot more concern now, especially that there might be potential opioids out on the market,” Pullman says. Regulations are trying to thread the needle between banning the plant and banning high-potency derivatives, knowing that when one derivative gets smacked down, another will quickly appear in its place. That cycle is a familiar one, mirroring the evolution and development of synthetic opioids.

“There’s risk with everything,” she says. “I think it’s important to distinguish the difference between a synthetic product versus the natural, and that way we can clearly attribute where the risk lies.”

A. Gour et al. Mislabeling and status of semisynthetic kratom-derived products in the US market. Drug Testing and Analysis. 2026. doi: 10.1002/dta.70122

#6443. Why did Earth stay hot for millions of years? Fossil shells offer a clue

A weaker carbon pump in the Southern Ocean may explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide during an ancient warm period.

The Southern Ocean helps move carbon from the atmosphere into the deep sea.

Around 50 million years ago, during one of Earth’s warmest periods in the past 66 million years, that process appears to have weakened.

Chemical traces in fossil shells suggest that microscopic plants at the ocean’s surface used a smaller share of the nutrients available to them than they did in cooler periods before and after.

That left more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, according to the study’s model.

The model suggests that the weaker carbon pump and the feedbacks it amplified could explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide at the time.

Simone Moretti of the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz, Germany, led the study. His co-authors came from the Université libre de Bruxelles (ULB), the University of California, Santa Cruz and other institutions.

“Our study shows that the Southern Ocean played a major role in regulating atmospheric CO2 during the early Eocene, millions of years before the onset of the recent ice ages,” Moretti said.

The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum ran from about 53 to 49 million years ago. Global temperatures were more than 18°F (10°C) higher than now, and carbon dioxide reached around 1,600 parts per million.

The causes of those levels are still debated. Volcanoes and reduced burial of organic carbon have both been proposed, but the timing of the eruptions lines up poorly with the warming.

So the team looked at the ocean’s biological carbon pump. Microscopic plants near the surface take up carbon dioxide as they grow. When they die, some of that carbon sinks and stays in the deep ocean for hundreds to thousands of years.

Today the pump runs below its full potential. Deep water rising around Antarctica brings up nutrients that the plants never fully use.

Plankton prefer the lighter form of nitrogen when they take up nitrate, their main nutrient. The more completely they use the supply, the heavier the leftover nitrogen becomes.

The nitrogen signature ends up in the shells of foraminifera, single-celled organisms that eat the plankton. The team measured the nitrogen trapped in fossil foraminifera from four sediment cores drilled by the Ocean Drilling Program.

Two cores came from the Southern Ocean. Two came from the mid-latitude Atlantic and Indian oceans, where nutrients are used up almost completely.

The gap between the two pairs of sites shows how much nutrient the Southern Ocean plants left behind. It was widest exactly when temperatures and carbon dioxide peaked, and it narrowed or vanished before and after.

The team then ran a simple model of the ocean and atmosphere using the estimated 40% drop in the share of available nutrients that plankton used.

On its own, the drop raised carbon dioxide from 700 to about 900 parts per million.

When the researchers included the effects of warming and changes in seawater chemistry, atmospheric carbon dioxide reached about 1,100 parts per million.

That increase accounts for about half of the roughly 800 parts per million rise reconstructed for the period.

The leak hit harder than it would today. Eocene seawater was more acidic and richer in calcium, so it had less capacity to absorb a change in carbon dioxide.

“Because Eocene seawater had a much lower capacity to buffer changes in CO2 than today’s ocean, a weakening of the biological carbon pump could have had a far greater impact on atmospheric CO2 than under present-day conditions,” said François Fripiat, a co-author at ULB.

Over millions of years, rain and rock weathering normally pull carbon dioxide back out of the air and act as a thermostat.

The early Eocene had no Alps or Himalayas yet, and its flat, deeply weathered continents offered little fresh rock.

“With Earth’s natural thermostat operating less efficiently, the additional CO2 released from the ocean could remain in the atmosphere for much longer,” said Mathis Hain, a co-author at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

“This would allow the Southern Ocean to influence climate not just over thousands of years, as during the ice ages, but over millions of years,” he said.

The Southern Ocean also released carbon dioxide during warm spells between recent ice ages.

The authors interpret the match across very different timescales as a sign of a dependable feedback.

The shells record that the plants left nutrients unused, but not why. Stronger mixing around Antarctica could have brought up more deep water, or the plants could have grown less.

The authors argued that iron supply, which limits plant growth there today, likely changed little in a warmer world. That leaves less room for the growth explanation.

The estimate of the nutrient drop is deliberately conservative, because one of the mid-latitude sites falls between the others in its values.

And the carbon model is a simple one, built to show the size of the effect rather than reproduce the Eocene ocean.

The open question is whether the modern Southern Ocean will respond the same way.

Simulations run for centuries to thousands of years suggest deep-water formation near Antarctica strengthens once the deep ocean catches up with surface warming, which would match the Eocene pattern.

The team is now exploring the same feedback in other periods of sustained warming. The paper names the Middle Eocene, the Middle Miocene and the Pliocene as candidates.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

#6442. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newfound genetic variant inherited from Neanderthals may shrink a part of modern-human brains without having any meaningful effects on mental ability, and it might also reduce the risk of schizophrenia, a new study finds.

"Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg, an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS.

Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. More than a decade of research has shown that Neanderthals and modern humans once interbred. Most people not of sub-Saharan ancestry living today possess about 2% Neanderthal ancestry.

Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. One reason for the differences has to do with the occipital lobe, the smallest of the brain's four lobes, which sits in the back of the skull. The occipital lobe houses the visual cortex, which helps process signals from the eyes. This area was relatively larger in Neanderthals than it is in modern humans.

In the new study, the researchers analyzed modern-human genomes for genetic variants that are related to occipital lobe size and were also likely inherited from Neanderthals. They discovered one such variant associated with the DAAM1 gene, which a 2019 study linked with brain development. This genetic variant was found only in modern humans outside Africa and was seen in five Neanderthal genomes.

Curiously, the Neanderthal variant the scientists detected in modern-human genomes led to an approximately 0.05-cubic-inch (0.85 cubic centimeters) reduction in occipital lobe size per copy of the variant in an individual. This means that the Neanderthal gene was linked to a slightly smaller brain size in modern humans.

A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk.

This effect is the opposite of what experts expected based on Neanderthals' large skull size, Tony Capra, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, it's important to remember that this one gene variant "does not reflect the full set of variations that might have been present in Neanderthals that might have affected the shape and size of their brain structures," Capra noted.

Zeberg and Pääbo also discovered that having two copies of the DAAM1 gene variant was associated with a nearly 10% reduction in the chances of having schizophrenia in modern humans. But there was no apparent link between the variant and intelligence in modern humans.

"A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk," Zeberg said.

Symptoms of schizophrenia can include altered perceptions of reality, such as visual hallucinations and problems with processing visual signals. This makes it "tempting to speculate" that this Neanderthal gene variant's effects on schizophrenia might be associated with the visual cortex. However, there is currently no evidence for such a link, Zeberg said.

Future research along these lines could analyze how other Neanderthal genetic variants influenced modern humans, Capra said, "to see if they had a consistent effect on us." Looking into Neanderthal variants that are missing from modern-human genomes could "show us what makes us modern humans as opposed to them," Capra added.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Zeberg, H., & Pääbo, S. (2026). A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(48). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2624837123
