#6439. What can AI learn from a thousand days of hearing what a baby hears?

Princeton recorded eight babies for their first 1,000 days, and a model trained on one child's audio learned language on the same schedule.

A toddler can pick up hundreds of words just by hearing people talk. Could a computer start from scratch and recognize many of those same words on roughly the same timetable?

Researchers at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute wired up 15 homes with cameras and microphones and recorded babies for most of their waking hours across the first 1,000 days of life.

The researchers turned speech recorded around eight children into clean audio using synthetic voices.

They trained a separate model on each child’s audio in the order the speech was originally recorded.

The models identified recurring sound patterns that corresponded to words.

On average, each model reached the halfway point on a vocabulary checklist within 22 days of the child it was paired with.

“We wanted to turn the usual logic of developmental research around,” said Uri Hasson, a professor of psychology and neuroscience at Princeton who led the study.

“Instead of observing a child for an hour in the laboratory, we asked whether we could build a model capable of learning and immerse it in the child’s actual experience, day after day.”

The families were in New Jersey and spanned a range of incomes and backgrounds. Each home got four to 14 recording devices spread across two to five rooms.

The devices ran 12 to 14 hours a day, from February 2022 to May 2025.

The project gathered roughly 1.2 million hours of audio and video, of which the eight homes analyzed in this paper supplied about 600,000. An automated pipeline worked out where the child was in the house and pulled out the speech happening nearby.

Each child ended up with between 1,900 and 6,600 hours of usable speech, three to seven and a half hours a day. That adds up to 6 to 27 million words per child, over a median of 960 recording days.

Every month from eight months on, caregivers filled out a standard checklist of which words their child understood and said. Those forms are how the researchers knew what each child knew, and when.

Children reached half of the 649-word checklist anywhere from about 12 to 22 months old. That ten-month spread between children is the thing most studies average away.

The model started from random numbers. It had no dictionary, no phonetics, no notion of where one word ends and the next begins, and no text.

The program’s first part chops the incoming sound into 20-millisecond pieces and sorts them into categories it invents for itself. Its second part tries to guess the next piece from what came before.

Whenever a run of pieces becomes reliably predictable, the program files it away as a unit, which is the closest thing it has to a word.

Nothing about that design is specific to English or even to speech. What makes it unusual is the schedule.

The audio arrives in the order it was recorded, one day at a time, rather than shuffled into batches the way an AI language model is normally trained.

At the end of each simulated day, the program gets a sample of speech from earlier days, weighted toward recent ones. The researchers call it replay.

English has 39 phonemes, the sound units that distinguish bat from pat. Children spend their first year tuning in to the ones their own language uses.

Within roughly 12 to 15 months of simulated time, the program had carved out dedicated categories for nearly all of them.

Across the eight children, the models averaged 37.5 phonemes each. The lowest count came from the household with the least recording.

The order it happened in, sounds before words, is the order infants follow.

Words came after. For the child the paper calls Coral, the checklist said she understood 97 words at 12 months, and her model had 91.

Across all eight children, the models and the children hit the same vocabulary milestones within an average of 22 days of each other, with the worst case 56 days.

The models also reproduced the differences between children, landing close to each child’s own halfway age.

They did not match perfectly. The models tended to start learning words a little late and then catch up faster, so the shape of the curve was only partly right.

The surprise in the paper is what happened when the researchers took replay away.

Coral’s household produced something like 10 million words a year, which is a rich environment by any measure. Hearing all of it once, in order, wasn’t enough. With a single pass the program barely learned words at all.

Around 25 to 30 passes over each day’s material was enough, and more than that added very little.

The researchers link this to what sleep is thought to do for memory. A program replaying audio files is not a sleeping infant, and the paper is careful about that.

The amount of recording mattered just as much. Fed only a tenth of Coral’s daily speech, under an hour a day, the program learned none of the checklist words by 24 months.

At 30% of the day, about two and a half hours, it learned 80 of the 649 checklist words.

At 70% it got about nine-tenths of the way to the full result. The rarer words, it seems, only turn up for a listener who is there most of the day.

One limitation shapes everything else. Household recordings are full of clattering dishes, television, and two people talking at once, and the program was not asked to cope with any of that.

Instead the researchers transcribed all the speech around each child, then had a text-to-speech system read the transcripts back as clean audio.

Each household got a mix of eight adult female voices, with 30% of segments read in a voice matched to the child’s mother.

So the word order, the timing and the vocabulary are real, and the sound isn’t. The acoustic problem a baby actually solves, picking one voice out of a noisy room, was left for later work.

Three of the eight children also had shorter recordings, 14 to 20 months of usable input, so their later trajectories are extrapolated rather than modeled.

The program also sees nothing: no faces, no pointing, no object being handed over, which is a large part of how toddlers work out what a word refers to.

The program learned sounds and words. It did not learn grammar, and whether the same machinery would arrive at sentence structure is the open question the authors name.

The team wants to use the setup for questions nobody can put to a real baby. What would less sleep do, or screen speech instead of a parent’s?

Future studies could also add eye contact and the rest of the social world the cameras captured but the model never saw.

Hadas Raviv, a computational cognitive scientist in Princeton’s psychology department who built the analysis pipeline, framed the goal as the opposite of the usual one in artificial intelligence.

“Unlike much of modern AI, which aims for superhuman performance, we’re trying to understand how humans learn and how that learning gives rise to intelligence,” Raviv said.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6437. Common fiber supplement eased knee arthritis pain and improved grip strength in six weeks

A six-week trial found that inulin fiber supplements modestly reduced knee osteoarthritis pain and improved grip strength in some adults.

Adults with knee osteoarthritis who took inulin, a fiber found in chicory root, ended a six-week trial with less knee pain than volunteers on a placebo. On a scale from zero to ten, their scores fell 1.11 points more.

Volunteers who took inulin alone also gained grip strength, a moderate effect. Those who followed a digital exercise program, or combined both treatments, did not.

The work was led by the University of Nottingham in England, and its results appeared in February 2026.

In 2019, about 528 million people worldwide were living with osteoarthritis, according to the World Health Organization. The knee is the joint most often affected, with 365 million cases.

About 33 million U.S. adults have the condition, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates. Physical exercise may help relieve pain and improve function, the agency notes.

In the U.K., 5.4 million people have knee osteoarthritis, according to a 2025 report from the charity Arthritis UK.

“Our recent lived experience survey showed that six in ten people are living in pain most or all of the time due to their arthritis,” said Professor Lucy Donaldson, the charity’s director of research.

Under its former name, Versus Arthritis, the charity was one of the trial’s funders.

Between May 2022 and February 2025, the researchers randomly assigned 136 adults to four groups, and 117 completed all assessments.

Those who finished averaged 67.5 years of age, and 58.1 percent were women.

One group took 0.7 ounces (20 grams) of inulin powder a day. A second followed Joint Academy, a digital physical therapy program that began with a call to a personal physical therapist.

A third group combined both, and a fourth took maltodextrin, a starch-based powder, as a placebo. For ethical reasons linked to blood sugar, the placebo dose was half the inulin dose.

Volunteers did not know whether they were taking inulin or the placebo, but those assigned to exercise knew it. The staff who measured outcomes were blinded to all treatments.

Inulin’s pain result only just reached statistical significance, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 0.04 to 2.18 points.

Exercise lowered pain scores by 1.55 points compared with placebo, and the combination by 1.67 points. No added benefit from combining the two emerged, though the sample was too small to reliably detect one.

On average, both single treatments exceeded the one-point drop that patients typically notice as meaningful. Exercise came close to the two-point threshold for feeling “much better.”

A third of placebo takers also improved by at least one point, but only 11 percent improved by two points or more.

Inulin made people less sensitive to pressure and to repeated painful stimuli, two measures linked to how the nervous system processes pain. Exercise alone had no such effect.

“This study raises the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change – adding a fibre supplement to your breakfast or yogurt – could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function,” said Dr. Afroditi Kouraki of the University of Nottingham’s School of Medicine, the lead author.

Exercise improved a timed up-and-go test and a 30-second chair-stand test. Inulin alone had no effect on either.

Inulin feeds gut bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids. Only inulin raised blood levels of butyrate, one of those fatty acids, and of GLP-1, a hormone made in the gut.

Within the inulin groups, higher GLP-1 was associated with better grip strength, in an exploratory analysis that needs independent replication. The authors offer no explanation for the combined group’s grip result.

“The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation,” said Professor Ana Valdes, the senior author, also of the School of Medicine.

A 2024 Canadian trial of a similar fiber in adults with knee osteoarthritis and obesity reported gains in grip strength and mobility after six months. Its effect on knee pain was only a trend.

The short duration may not capture the full effects of exercise, the researchers acknowledged. Expectation effects in the exercise groups cannot be ruled out either.

Dropout reached 21 percent in the two exercise groups, compared with 3.6 percent in the two groups without exercise. To compensate, allocation odds were shifted toward exercise during later recruitment, which may have introduced bias.

A second analysis that included dropouts, with missing scores statistically imputed, gave consistent results. Only the effect of exercise on the up-and-go test lost statistical significance.

Of 50 inulin takers who finished, 23 reported minor digestive effects such as wind and bloating. None stopped the supplement or dropped out because of them.

U.K. government guidelines cited by the National Health Service call for 1.1 ounces (30 grams) of fiber a day, so the inulin dose alone supplied two-thirds of that.

Valdes sits on the scientific advisory boards of the nutrition company Chuckling Goat and of OLIPOP, roles declared unrelated to this study.

The study was published in the journal Nutrients.

#6436. The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The virus, eliminated in 2000, has now been circulating for more than a year

Flyers provide information about a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County aiming to curb an ongoing outbreak.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO announced; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

“To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”

PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

That measles made a comeback is not a surprise, says Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and quickly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”

But surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo said. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

Homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, says Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

Measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento says. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer said in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive plan at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo says. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

There’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has said the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”

Eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo says. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”

Public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in New Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also announced that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”

#6435. Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

On Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. Here, we look back at its most important discoveries, seen through groundbreaking space photos.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

The growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

"What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong."

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

NASA's Voyager 2 probe launched before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.)

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about."

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month

The close-up view showed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

While passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker said. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking."

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any big craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker said.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km)

Some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image

A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker said, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture."

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five new moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This showed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

By 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot."

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker said. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is."

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image

Voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating."

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. #6434. The next ice age may have begun 2,000 years ago, but humans cut it short

Buried plants on Baffin Island reveal when a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet began growing again and how human-caused warming reversed its advance.

About 2,000 years ago, the last remnant of the ice sheet that once covered much of Canada began growing again on Baffin Island.

It expanded in bursts, then began retreating around 1960 as warmer summers melted more ice than winters added.

The researchers argue that the regrowth marked the earliest stage of a new glaciation in North America, and that human-caused warming cut it short.

At the peak of the last glacial period, the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered much of Canada and reached into the northern United States.

“People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” said Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory who led the study.

What’s left of it is the Barnes Ice Cap, on the central plateau of Baffin Island in Nunavut. Its bedrock is low for the Canadian Arctic, only about 1,640 feet (500 meters) above sea level.

The ice has lasted this long because it is roughly 2,300 feet (700 meters) thick, enough to lift its surface to where snow survives the summer.

Young’s team wanted to know whether the ice cap had ever been smaller than it is today and then grown back. Gifford Miller of the University of Colorado Boulder was among the co-authors.

The answer matters beyond one ice cap, because models say glaciations over North America most likely begin on Baffin Island.

The Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the rock beneath it, so it doesn’t slide the way most glaciers do. Instead of grinding the ground as it spreads, it buries whatever is growing there and preserves it.

When the margin retreats, the moss and small plants it killed centuries ago come out of the ice.

Radiocarbon dating estimates when the plants died, giving researchers a way to date the ice’s advance.

Young’s team collected 88 of those plants at or near the 2022 ice edge. About 70% of them died around the year 1800, give or take 200 years. Those were the coldest summers of the Little Ice Age.

Sixteen more came from a half-mile (800-meter) line running out from the ice edge. A drained lake there had let the margin retreat farther than anywhere else.

In an interview with Earth.com, Young said that result surprised the team.

The researchers hadn’t expected the ice cap to have been smaller than it is now at any point in the last several thousand years.

“This unique finding allowed us to unexpectedly use these plants to track the ice cap’s renewed expansion,” Young noted.

The researchers also dated 35 boulders and bedrock surfaces around the ice cap. Rock that is open to the sky builds up a rare form of beryllium at a known rate.

The amount in a surface tells how long it has been uncovered.

All of the surfaces gave the same answer: the old ice sheet had retreated inside its 2022 position about 3,600 years ago.

The oldest plants along the half-mile line died around the year 1000, so the ice was already advancing by then.

To fill the gap, the team turned to 186 radiocarbon dates from plants under smaller ice caps on the same plateau. Not one of those dates is older than the Common Era.

The authors read that as the moment, roughly 2,000 years ago, when the summer snowline dropped onto the plateau and ice began to build up across it.

So the Laurentide reached its smallest size between about 3,000 and 2,000 years ago and then started to grow. The authors count that reversal as the start of the next glaciation.

The ice advanced in pulses during cold spells and was nearing its largest modern extent by about 1800.

By 1960 the growth had stopped. Aerial photographs show the margin retreating from about 1961, and the ice cap has since given up between 650 and 2,600 feet (200 and 800 meters) of ground.

Snow also survives the summer on less and less of it.

Around 1960, about 35% of its surface was high enough for snow to last through the summer. By the early 2000s only 3% was, and since 2010 none of it has been.

There is no longer any part of the ice cap where snow can pile up and turn into ice.

Summer temperatures have been climbing since the late 1700s, and since the early 1960s warmer summers account for almost all of the ice cap’s losses. Those summers track the greenhouse gases people have added to the air.

Between 1750 and 1850, the total rose by only about 12 parts per million of carbon dioxide equivalent. By 1960 it had risen another 50, and by 2024 another 138.

“The expansion and retreat of ice sheets has been one of Earth’s most consistent patterns over the last 2.6 million years,” Young told Earth.com.

About 2,000 years ago, he said, the Laurentide was starting its next phase of expansion, as it should have. Then greenhouse gases ended that expansion in the middle of the 20th century.

In the 1970s, some climate scientists argued that a new ice age was coming, and the idea got a famous airing in Newsweek.

Young said those scientists were essentially correct, even if the media twisted the story. “We did just barely start the next glaciation, but they didn’t know it at the time,” he said.

Behind that growth was a slow decline in summer sunlight at high northern latitudes, the orbital rhythm that paces ice ages.

Greenhouse gases did rise over those thousands of years, by about 20 parts per million. The authors found that was too small to overcome the cooling.

Computer models suggest the next glaciation will not begin for thousands of years. But those models usually define its start as the point where new ice sheets hold enough ice to lower the sea by about 10 feet (3 meters) or more.

Young’s team said that would miss the earlier stage of ice growth that his team considers the start of a glaciation.

A 2025 study built from ocean sediments and Earth’s orbit estimated that the first regrowth of ice in this interglacial would come somewhere in the last 1,800 years or so. The plants on Baffin Island agree.

What the record can’t yet say is exactly when the regrowth began. The plants that would date it are still under the ice, and only continued retreat will bring them out.

The dates so far are archived at the NSF Arctic Data Center.

Young said models of the ice cap’s future have it disappearing completely within the next few hundred years.

Asked what happens once the last piece of the Laurentide is gone, Young said another glaciation is unlikely anytime soon.

“Given the amount of greenhouse gases that are in the atmosphere and that we continue to pump, the next glaciation is a long way off,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6432. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

#6431. Eleven pregnant garter snakes went to a San Francisco zoo, and now 62 of their young are in the wild

62 endangered San Francisco garter snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were released in San Mateo County this fall, the first head-start release.

In spring 2025, U.S. Geological Survey biologists caught 11 pregnant San Francisco garter snakes on the San Mateo County coast, in a preserve run by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen).

They took them to the San Francisco Zoo, where the snakes gave birth later that year.

After giving birth, the mothers were returned to the wild, the zoo says. The zoo’s team raised their young until they were big enough to be released.

On November 10, 2026, the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens said 62 of those zoo-born garter snakes had been released this fall in San Mateo County.

It was the first release under a head-starting program for the endangered subspecies. The announcement does not say how many are still alive.

The San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia) is a subspecies of the common garter snake. The zoo says it lives only in San Mateo County and a small corner of Santa Cruz County.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes red on the top of the head, a greenish-blue or blue belly, a wide pale stripe down the back and red and black stripes on the sides.

A major loss of habitat came after World War II. In the 1940s, the sag ponds along Skyline Boulevard, small ponds in low spots along a fault line, held hundreds of the snakes.

By the 1960s, nearly all of those ponds had been drained and built over, according to the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy.

The snake went onto the first federal endangered species list on March 11, 1967, six years before the Endangered Species Act of 1973. The zoo estimates that a couple thousand remain in the wild today.

Federal biologists blame illegal collection, construction, drought and saltwater in coastal ponds. Bullfrogs and largemouth bass are on the list too, because they eat the snakes and their prey.

That prey includes threatened California red-legged frogs, which the snakes rely on for food, the zoo says.

Since 2004, the conservancy and the National Park Service have restored and enhanced 33 acres (13 hectares) of wetland, grassland and coastal scrub for the snakes, according to Midpen’s 2025 release. The work added new ponds for breeding habitat.

Garter snakes give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. In this subspecies, birth comes in July or August. A litter can hold 6 to 35 babies, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile says.

After the 11 females arrived, the team scanned them with ultrasound. The early scans showed that a goal of 80 to 120 live babies was feasible, Midpen reported in September 2025.

Later that month, the district estimated that the zoo’s Conservation Team was raising about 120 newborns.

The zoo had practice with the species. Its staff bred San Francisco garter snakes in the 1990s to work out how to keep them.

From 2005, they developed care protocols with the San Diego Zoo on housing, diet, growth tracking and parasite checks, Midpen said in 2025.

Rochelle Stiles, the zoo’s director of field conservation, described the goal of the zoo’s snake rearing work.

“By providing these young snakes with a safe environment during their most vulnerable stage of life, we’re giving them a stronger start in the wild,” she said.

Head-starting works that way. The young are fed and sheltered until they are big enough to handle predators and competition for food, a method that also saved an endangered wallaby population in Australia.

Each snake born at the zoo had a genetic test before it left, and the results set its destination. About one-third went back to the area where its mother had been caught.

The rest went to several other populations that were short on both snakes and genetic variety. Isolated groups slowly lose diversity, the same problem behind a proposed genetic rescue for Lassen red foxes in northern California.

Disease data mattered too. Laura Patterson coordinates amphibian and reptile conservation statewide for the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).

She said a CDFW survey for snake fungal disease, an emerging disease found in many wild snakes, “aided in the selection process.”

The partners will not name the release sites. The zoo said secrecy protects the snakes from collectors, cars and disease.

Midpen biologist Karine Tokatlian also commented on the release. “Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” she said.

Removal from the endangered list requires at least 10 viable, self-sustaining breeding populations. Each one needs at least 200 snakes.

U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) ecologists had already tested the idea on a computer. In a 2023 paper in PLOS ONE, a team led by Jonathan Rose of the USGS Western Ecological Research Center simulated new populations started with newborns, juveniles, adults or a mix.

Head-started juveniles gave those populations the best chance of lasting. Releases would have to continue for at least 15 years to keep the risk of near-extinction low, the model said.

Raising juveniles also takes fewer adults away from the donor site. Justin Sloan, acting deputy field supervisor at the USFWS Sacramento office, credited research, genetic testing, habitat work and specialized care.

Ariel Starr, a Midpen wildlife ecologist, looked beyond this one subspecies.

“The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species,” she said.

The November announcement gives no survival rate for the 62. It also does not say how long they had been out when it was posted.

Survival is low even for snakes born in the wild. One study found only 2 percent of females born live to age 5, according to the USFWS.

There is also a gap between the 2025 estimate of about 120 newborns and the 62 released. The zoo did not explain it.

The 2023 model focused on snake demography. Its authors wrote that the genetics of the donor, captive and released snakes would also be a major concern for any reintroduction plan.

More than 130 garter snakes were born at the zoo in 2026. They are being raised for a second round of releases in 2027. Monitoring of both rounds will show whether the populations at the sites grow.

Rachel Townsend, a National Park Service wildlife biologist, put the first round in proportion. “Releasing these snakes is a significant moment, but it is one step of many in a much larger recovery effort,” she said.

The mothers are back in the wild. This fall, 62 of their young were let go at sites the partners will not name.

The information was obtained from the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens.

Space and time seem like the bedrock of reality. But startling clues are leading physicists toward the possibility that something stranger lies beneath.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every experience we have and every moment we live unfold naturally across space and time ‪—‬ so naturally that we rarely stop to question their existence.

Physics takes this just as much for granted as we do. For more than 100 years, the field has been built upon the foundational idea that space-time — the four-dimensional fabric of the universe — is fundamental.

But new insights drawn from the hearts of black holes, quantum computers and ultraprecise lasers, are now poised to challenge this assumption, leading a growing number of physicists to ask the same question: What if space and time aren't the bedrock of the universe, but emerge from something even deeper?

"You can build space from a theory without space," Jeff Forshaw, a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester in the U.K., told Live Science.

For decades, we have known that two extraordinarily successful descriptions of nature are incompatible.

In Einstein's general theory of relativity, matter and energy bend space-time and we experience that curvature as gravity. Quantum mechanics, meanwhile, describes nature on the smallest scales of atoms and subatomic particles.

But quantum mechanics still has no adequate description of the force of gravity. The conflict between these theories of big and small becomes unavoidable in extreme environments, such as the centers of black holes or the smallest fractions of a second after the Big Bang, where gravity grows to be intense on the minute scales ruled by quantum mechanics.

An artist's illustration of the Big Bang with time running from the image's bottom to the top. During the first brief fraction of a second after the Big Bang the universe was so dense that quantum effects and gravity were equally strong.

So far, efforts to combine them mathematically and theoretically have led to nonsensical results.

"They seem not to fit together into a single, consistent framework that we know to be correct," Latham Boyle, a theoretical physicist at the University of Edinburgh in the U.K, told Live Science.

It's possible that one or both of these theories is incomplete, but an increasingly popular belief among physicists is that both theories are perched upon an untested assumption: space-time itself.

Both general relativity and quantum mechanics assume that space-time exists. Yet neither explains why our universe seems to have three dimensions of space and one of time, or where space-time comes from. If this assumption is wrong, the apparent foundation of reality could be a large-scale approximation of something even more mysterious.

In Einstein's model, space-time is a little like how people once viewed water: smooth and continuous, capable of bending and rippling. But water only appears continuous on large scales because we can't see its composite "bits," or individual molecules, said Boyle, whose research explores quantum gravity, the early universe and whether space-time is fundamental or emergent. One proposal is that space-time is similar.

"It seems smooth but only because we can't view it under a fine enough microscope," Boyle told Live Science. Yet no one has found direct evidence for space-time's microscopic "bits." That leaves physicists searching for indirect clues in places where existing theories are pushed to their breaking point: black holes.

At the hearts of black holes, general relativity breaks down by predicting space-time curving infinitely, while quantum physics gives their boundaries baffling properties.

Around black holes gravity (the curvature of space-time) is warped to an infinite degree.

Black holes also offer intriguing clues that space-time, like water, may have microscopic ingredients. One clue comes from thermodynamics ‪—‬ the laws governing heat, temperature and entropy.

Entropy is often described as measuring the disorder in a system, but physicists use it to describe how many hidden microscopic arrangements can produce the same large-scale behavior. A glass of water, for example, may have one temperature and pressure even though its molecules could be moving and arranged in an enormous number of different ways. The more possible microscopic arrangements there are, the greater its entropy.

This matters because thermodynamics usually describes the large-scale behavior of microscopic ingredients. If Einstein’s equations are thermodynamic in nature, their entropy may be due to hidden microscopic states of space-time that physicists cannot yet see.

"General relativity is thermodynamics," Forshaw said. "Einstein's equations are a statement of thermodynamics. They're a statistically emergent feature of an underlying theory."

In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that black holes, too, have entropy and a physical temperature. This raised striking questions: Are there microscopic ingredients that account for those thermodynamic properties, and if so, what are they?

If those constituents exist, then space-time's smooth geometry, like the continuous appearance of water, emerges only on larger scales.

Another clue is that Einstein's equations appear to contain traces of this hidden structure, somehow reproducing the relationships needed for black holes to have a temperature, even though the theory directly connects the shape of space-time only to the matter it contains.

"Einstein's equation, which we thought was just a classical equation, nothing to do with quantum mechanics, seems to secretly know — or at some level to have known — about this finite entropy associated with the black hole," Boyle said.

The entropy of black holes also gives rise to a second sign that space-time emerges from something deeper: a puzzle known as the black hole information paradox.

Stephen Hawking in front of a projection of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula for black holes.

Quantum mechanics says that physical information can never be destroyed. Yet if black holes emit radiation — an idea famously proposed by Stephen Hawking in 1974 — they should slowly evaporate. This is a profound contradiction: A black hole's Hawking radiation is thermal, depending solely on its mass, electric charge and angular momentum. It contains no obvious record of what originally fell inside. That means that if the black hole eventually disappears, the information of what it once gobbled up seems to vanish with it.

But a black hole's entropy scales not with the three-dimensional volume enclosed by it but with the two-dimensional area of its event horizon, the point beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Therefore, it's possible that all the information within any region might somehow be stored on its boundary. This became known as the holographic principle, named after a hologram, in which a 3D image is encoded on a 2D surface.

In 1997, theoretical physicist Juan Maldacena made the idea mathematically precise. He showed that a higher-dimensional theory containing gravity could be mapped onto a lower-dimensional quantum theory without it.

The two descriptions appeared to be interchangeable, equally valid views of reality. But some researchers now go further: They think the lower-dimensional quantum theory may be the fundamental description, while the higher-dimensional space-time we seem to live in is what emerges when its information is decoded.

These ideas gave rise to holography. Its central principle is that a gravitational world in more dimensions may be completely encoded by a quantum theory without gravity in fewer dimensions. That lower-dimensional theory lives on the boundary of the higher-dimensional spacetime.

You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real

Mark Van Raamsdonk, a professor of physics at the University of British Columbia, compares the concept to a computer's memory chip. At the fundamental level, a video game is encoded in physical bits switching between states. Yet on a screen, those bits produce a representation of a 3D world containing objects, movement and physical rules. The virtual world seems spatially real, even though its underlying information is stored very differently.

"You should think of the lower-dimensional thing as being what's most real," Van Raamsdonk told Live Science.

Quantum entanglement may play a central role in how this lower-dimensional information gives rise to higher-dimensional space-time. It describes how particles can share linked quantum properties, even when separated by vast distances.

"If I want to decode what space-time geometry is being stored by the quantum state of this lower-dimensional system, all I need to do is probe this entanglement structure," Van Raamsdonk said.

For decades, directly testing this theory appeared hopeless. Physicists thought they would need particle collisions approaching the Planck scale — the fantastically high energy at which quantum effects are expected to become as important as gravity, and far beyond anything existing colliders can produce.

But physicists realized they don't need to rely on brute force. They are now developing several ways around that energy barrier.

The CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. Reaching the Planck scale requires roughly 900 trillion times more energy than the Large Hadron Collider can produce.

How could scientists discover whether space-time has a deeper structure? One way is to search for a subtle jitter, or static hum, in space-time itself. Experiments such as GQuEST, a collaboration involving Fermilab and Caltech, and QUEST at Cardiff University in the U.K. split laser light along different paths and recombine it. Extraordinarily small changes in the distance light travels may reveal fluctuations, arising from discrete building blocks of space-time, that are consistent with some of holography's models.

In some holographic models, physicists represent the underlying units of information as quantum bits (qubits) — mathematically identical to those used in quantum computers. Physically, a computer qubit may be encoded in an ion or electrical circuit, whereas a qubit in a holographic model represents a possible microscopic unit of the quantum theory from which space-time emerges. This equivalence allows quantum processors to simulate space-time models.

In such models, the patterns of entanglement between the qubits dictate the physical distances between regions of space. The stronger those entanglements are, the closer together two corresponding regions are; if the entanglements are severed, the space-time between them tears apart.

QUEST compares measurements from two neighboring laser beam splitters, or interferometers. Some theoretical models predict quantum fluctuations of space-time that would affect both instruments in a related way. Researchers therefore search for matching fluctuations in their measurements while working to rule out shared sources of laboratory noise. Finding the predicted pattern could support those models; finding nothing would constrain how strong such fluctuations could be, killing off flawed models and refining how microscopic components (or chunks of information) translate into space-time's geometry.

Atom interferometers such as AION and MAGIS-100 extend the search for quantum jitters by using atoms as sensitive probes. When a laser pulse hits an atom, the atom enters superposition, in which it is simultaneously in two different locations at once. It then travels along two separate paths before being recombined by a final pulse. If space-time fluctuates slightly differently along one path than the other, a measurable shift is detected in the atom's interference pattern.

The cold-atom preparation and trapping apparatus for the strontium atom source in Fermilab's Matter-wave Atomic Gradiometer Interferometric Sensor (MAGIS-100).

Another approach called BMV experiments (after the surnames of their independent developers Sougato Bose and his collaborators, Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral) take diamond nanocrystals weighing around a hundred-billonth of a kilogram and place them into a state of quantum superposition.

Painstakingly shielded from every possible electromagnetic and nuclear interaction, and placed at different distances from one another, the diamonds are put through a key test. If they emerge from the experiment with the electron states entangled, then gravity alone produced the entanglement.

That would be evidence that gravity can transmit quantum effects — something a classical gravitational field could not produce. And if gravity (the curvature of space-time) can exist in superposition, it could be a strong clue that space-time's geometry is woven out of quantum information. The challenge, so far, is in excluding all the other effects that may obscure the signal.

On cosmic scales, future gravitational wave observatories ‪—‬ including the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer ‪—‬ could scrutinize gravity at the first clues' source: around black holes. After two black holes merge, the resulting object settles down by emitting gravitational waves with characteristic frequencies and decay times. Einstein's theory makes precise predictions for this "ringdown," allowing researchers to search for discrepancies.

An artist's illustration for how the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect ripples in space-time created by merging black holes.

Such discrepancies could potentially point to the quantum nature of space-time near black holes. Interpreting them would require distinguishing between competing explanations ‪—‬ an unexpected signal could cryptically hint at space-time's underlying nature, but it wouldn't reveal a direct picture of its microscopic ingredients.

To identify the bits that make up the reality beneath space-time, scientists are also turning to quantum computers. By entangling many qubits in specific ways to mimic different models of emergent space-time, scientists could determine which mathematical models of the constituent bits are more likely.

"The study of many-body, highly entangled systems is where the future of this whole enterprise is," Forshaw said.

Precursor tests are already underway. In 2022, for example, Google's Sycamore quantum processor was used to reproduce the behavior of a simple theoretical wormhole — not by creating a real hole in space-time but by arranging nine qubits so that their behavior could also be described using gravity.

Earlier this year, researchers went further, using the trapped-ion quantum computer IonQ Forte to test how something resembling gravitational geometry could emerge from patterns of quantum information. The qubits in Forte were arranged into a model that could be interpreted in two connected ways: both as a network of quantum information and as a simple holographic geometry. The researchers then altered the entanglement between the qubits. In the model’s gravitational interpretation, this was akin to adding mass. Just as adding mass bends Einstein's space-time, the researchers expected changing the entanglement to alter the corresponding geometry — and it did.

The findings demonstrate that researchers can study a mathematical relationship between entanglement and geometry using quantum hardware. However, they do not establish that our space-time emerges from lower-dimensional quantum information.

"The experiment that we did is a baby step in that direction," Crystal Noel, an experimental physicist at Duke University who led the experimental side of the project, told Live Science. One limitation of this result is that it reproduces features of a simplified, static theoretical universe, rather than the expanding universe in which we live. Testing a more realistic model of the universe might require entangling 100 or 200 qubits, which may be possible in the near future.

Each of these experiments will probe different aspects of the relationship between gravity and quantum physics, although none would by itself prove that space-time emerges from information. Taken together, however, their results could begin to reveal what theories of quantum gravity match the real world — and whether emergent space-time is among them.

Such a discovery would raise profound questions not only about the universe’s foundations, but about what it means for anything — including ourselves — to exist within it.

"If I tell you that space doesn't exist, it really questions what it means to be," Forshaw said. "How can you actually talk about things when there's no space to put things in?"

Alex Keshavarzi is a senior research fellow in particle physics at University College London in the U.K., where he is probing how the behaviors of muons (the heavier cousins of electrons) could reveal unknown particles and forces.
